scope_justification: A human-made document or structured record that captures details of a safety-related event: what happened, when, where, who was affected, root causes identified, and corrective actions taken. Built to persist information about safety events for analysis, compliance, and organizational learning.

Human-made quantifiable indicators used to measure, track, and evaluate the state and effectiveness of safety systems. Built to persist through systematic data collection, recording, and reporting — enabling evidence-based safety decisions by converting raw safety data into actionable measures.

A human-made visual interface that consolidates safety metrics, indicators, and operational data into a single display surface for monitoring and decision-making. Built to persist through software implementation and operational maintenance.

A human-made framework that categorizes and evaluates the developmental stage of an organization's safety management system across progressively advanced levels. Built to persist through published models, assessment tools, and organizational self-evaluation practices.

A formal approval gate in safety-critical industries (aerospace, nuclear, medical devices, construction) where designated authorities certify that all safety requirements for a phase or product have been met before work may proceed to the next stage. It is a human-made institutional mechanism for controlling risk through documented authorization.

A human-made measure, device, or procedure designed to eliminate, reduce, or mitigate a hazard to an acceptable level. It is an institutional artifact — part of the safety management system — that specifies what actions, technologies, or organizational arrangements are deployed to manage risk.

A human-made, measurable goal established by an organization to improve safety performance within a defined timeframe. It specifies what level of risk reduction or safety improvement is to be achieved, expressed in quantifiable terms such as incident rates, training completion percentages, or control effectiveness metrics. Safety targets are institutional artifacts of safety management systems, distinct from natural risk levels.

A human-made system of observation and measurement designed to track safety performance indicators, detect hazards, and verify compliance with safety procedures. It persists through instruments, protocols, and reporting mechanisms built to produce ongoing situational awareness.

A human-made category for events where safety controls or barriers failed, were bypassed, or proved insufficient — resulting in actual harm, near-miss, or property damage. It persists through documentation, investigation processes, and institutional memory that transforms raw events into learnable data.

A human-made capability to link safety-relevant information — decisions, test results, incidents, design changes — across the full lifecycle of a system. It persists through audit trails, configuration management databases, and version-controlled documentation that maintain referential links between safety artifacts.

A human-made systematic process of establishing documented confidence that safety requirements are consistently met throughout a system's lifecycle. It persists through audits, reviews, independent verification, and compliance programs that track assurance activities from design through decommissioning.

A human-built structured repository that organizes, stores, and retrieves safety-related information — procedures, incident reports, risk assessments, lessons learned, and best practices — enabling organizations to maintain institutional memory and support safety-management decisions through searchable, version-controlled documentation.

A human-built systematic process of examining systems, components, or procedures under controlled or simulated conditions to verify they meet specified safety requirements and performance standards before deployment or continued operation

A human-built modeling technique that reproduces system conditions — operational, fault, or emergency — in a controlled environment to examine how safety behaviors manifest, test responses, and predict failure modes before real-world deployment.

Safety-readiness is a human-made organizational state describing the preparedness level for handling safety incidents. It is built through structured training, drills, simulations, and assessments — designed to persist as an ongoing capability that can be measured, maintained, and improved over time.

Safety-resilience is a human-made organizational capability describing the ability of safety systems and processes to absorb disturbances, adapt to changing conditions, and recover functionality after disruptions. It is built through adaptive training, redundancy design, learning mechanisms, and organizational flexibility — deliberately engineered to persist beyond static safety measures.

A human-made governance practice that verifies organizational processes, systems, and behaviors conform to established safety requirements, standards, and regulations — built to persist through structured audits, documentation, and reporting mechanisms

The human-made process of establishing safety objectives, identifying hazards in advance, and designing controls before work begins. Safety planning produces documented plans, procedures, and organizational frameworks that guide all subsequent safety activities. It is a deliberate, forward-looking activity that structures how organizations prevent harm rather than merely respond to it.

The human-made construct of evaluating and classifying the sophistication, integration, and continuous improvement of an organization's safety management practices across defined levels of development.

The human-made concept of a breach or failure in safety controls, procedures, or vigilance — a moment when risk exposure increases due to human error, procedural deviation, or systemic weakness in the safety system.

The human-made practice of restoring operations and wellbeing after a safety incident — encompassing emergency response, damage mitigation, operational resumption, and post-event stabilization. Built to persist through documented procedures, incident action plans, and trained response teams that activate when normal safety controls have failed.

The human-made practice of communicating hazards, alerts, and safety information to relevant parties through standardized warnings, alarms, and notifications. Built to persist through engineered alert systems, protocol-defined escalation chains, and institutional awareness training.

The human-made practice of embedding safety considerations into the design, development, and operation of complex systems — making safety constitutive rather than additive. Built to persist through engineering standards, design methodologies, and safety-by-design frameworks.

A human-made conceptual framework for identifying, classifying, and managing risks that threaten human health, physical integrity, or well-being. It emerges from the practice of assessing hazards in engineered systems, workplaces, and environments, and persists through risk registers, assessment protocols, and regulatory frameworks that standardize how societies quantify and respond to threats to safety.

a human-made practice of systematically examining incidents, accidents, and near-misses after they occur to determine root causes and lessons learned, built to persist through formal procedures, reporting systems, and institutional knowledge

Safety-architecture is a human-made structured framework that organizes safety principles, controls, and governance arrangements into a coherent design. It specifies how safety requirements are decomposed, allocated, and verified across system components and organizational layers. The concept persists through engineering standards, safety case frameworks, and regulatory compliance structures that codify the architecture's structure and evolution.

A human-made process framework that structures safety activities across the stages of a system's existence — from conception through design, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning. It is built to persist as a discipline of systematic risk management across engineering, operational, and organizational contexts.

Predefined safety objectives that guide an organization's safety management system — human-made targets for reducing risk, established through standards (e.g. ISO 45001), policy documents, and organizational practice. They persist through written documentation, regulatory frameworks, and sustained managerial commitment.

Human-made practice of structured teaching and knowledge transfer on safety principles, procedures, and hazard awareness — distinct from general safety-training by its focus on specific, task-relevant safety content delivered in a focused, often brief format (e.g. toolbox talks, shift briefings, pre-task instructions). Built to persist through documented procedures, training materials, and organizational practice.

Safety performance is the measurable level of safety achievement in an organization or system, assessed through indicators, metrics, and evaluation against established safety objectives and regulatory requirements. It is a human-made construct used in safety management systems to track, measure, and communicate how well safety controls and processes are working.

A structured communication event where safety-relevant information — hazards, controls, emergency procedures — is conveyed to personnel before a task, shift, or project phase. Human-made through scheduled practice, checklists, and documentation protocols; persists through institutional memory and repeatable format.

An institutional mechanism assigning responsibility for safety outcomes and requiring answerability when those outcomes fall short. Human-made through formal charters, role descriptions, and organizational hierarchies that bind individuals and units to safety performance — not a natural tendency but a designed governance structure.

A human-made management construct: a quantifiable measure used to evaluate and communicate an organization's or individual's performance against explicitly defined strategic objectives. Built to persist through organizational reporting systems, business literature, and managerial practice.

A human-made organizational practice: the structured process by which workplace incidents, near-misses, and unsafe conditions are documented, analysed, and reported within a safety management system. Built to persist through written procedures, reporting tools, and regulatory requirements that turn raw events into institutional knowledge.

A human-made concept in safety engineering describing the condition where safety measures, barriers, or controls fail to prevent a hazardous event from occurring. The map distinguishes between different modes of failure (latent, active, systemic) and tracks how failures cascade through complex systems. Built to persist through standards (IEC 61508, ISO 45001), incident investigations, and safety-critical system design practice.

A safety-gate is a human-made decision point embedded in a project or product lifecycle, where compliance with safety requirements is formally evaluated before the project may proceed to the next stage. Built to persist through governance frameworks, checklists, and regulatory mandates, it institutionalizes the principle that safety must be verified at critical junctures rather than added retrospectively.

a visual representation that shows the sequence of steps, decisions, and data flow in a process; built as a communication and documentation tool for mapping and analyzing workflows across engineering, operations, and software development

a structured, organization-wide framework for managing safety through policies, procedures, training, and continuous improvement — built to persist through governance structures and sustained organizational practice

a measure of confidence that a safety-related system will perform its required safety functions correctly under all required conditions; built to persist through functional safety standards (IEC 61508/61511), certification regimes, and regulatory compliance frameworks

A human-made assessment framework that classifies components, failure modes, or processes by their importance to overall system safety. Created through hazard analysis and risk assessment methods to prioritize safety resources and determine required assurance levels. Persisted in safety cases, regulatory standards (IEC 61508, ISO 26262), and certification documents.

A human-made evaluation instrument that measures the shared attitudes, beliefs, values, and behavioral norms regarding safety within an organization or group. Created through surveys, interviews, and observational tools designed by safety professionals to diagnose cultural strengths and weaknesses in safety management.

A human-made measurement construct that tracks proactive safety activities and conditions before harm occurs — such as training completion rates, safety observations conducted, or hazard reports submitted. Created through safety management systems and maintained by periodic data collection.

A human-made measurement construct that tracks actual harm events and their precursors after they occur — such as incident counts, injury rates, near-miss reports, and equipment failures — providing retrospective data on safety performance.

A human-made system of conveying information about workplace hazards — including labels, safety data sheets, warnings, and training — designed to ensure workers understand the risks they face and how to protect themselves

A human-made construct representing a broad, high-level aim for safety performance within an organization or system. Safety goals are set by management as part of a safety management framework and provide direction for all safety-related activities, from risk assessment to incident prevention. They are deliberately framed broadly to endure across operational cycles and organizational changes.
a human-made standard or requirement established to evaluate safety conditions, performance, or compliance; created by regulators, organizations, or standards bodies to set measurable benchmarks

a human-made set of standardized procedures, rules, and practices established to ensure safety in operations; created by organizations, regulators, or standards bodies and enforced through documentation, training, and monitoring to prevent harm

a human-made standard or specification that establishes requirements, guidelines, or characteristics for safety-related products, processes, systems, or practices; created by standards bodies, regulatory agencies, or industry groups to ensure consistent levels of safety across organizations and jurisdictions

a human-made structured list of items, steps, or verification points used to ensure safety procedures are completed correctly and consistently; created by organizations as a tool to prevent omission of critical safety actions during complex or high-risk operations

a human-made practice of structured instruction and knowledge transfer designed to develop specific competencies, skills, or awareness; organized through curricula, programs, and pedagogical methods that persist across institutions and generations

a human-made practice of involving workers in safety-related decisions, hazard identification, and policy development; organized through safety committees, consultation procedures, and reporting systems that give workers formal roles in maintaining workplace safety

a human-made practice of collecting, analyzing, and communicating safety performance data back to stakeholders — workers, managers, auditors — to inform decisions and drive continuous improvement; organized through structured loops linking incident reports, observations, audits, and metrics to the people who can act on them
a human-made practice where an experienced guide works one-on-one with a learner to develop skills, improve performance, and build self-directed capability through dialogue and feedback

a human-made concept: the systematic cognitive recognition of hazards, risks, and unsafe conditions in one's environment; built to persist through communication campaigns, signage, drills, and organizational learning

A human-made institutional practice and normative standard requiring information to be accessible, visible, and disclosed to stakeholders. Built to persist through laws, regulations, open-records systems, publication requirements, and disclosure norms that actively construct visibility where opacity would naturally arise.

A human-made measurement construct designed to predict future outcomes by tracking activities, conditions, or early signals that precede a target result. Built to persist through analytical frameworks, dashboards, and management practice across safety, business, healthcare, and operations.

A human-made measurement construct designed to record and quantify past outcomes, events, or results after they have occurred. Built to persist through reports, statistics, and historical records used for assessment and learning across safety, business, healthcare, and operations.

A human-made measurement construct designed to track the critical variables that signal organizational success or failure. Built to persist through dashboards, reporting frameworks, and management systems that translate strategy into measurable targets.

a human-made safety management concept that establishes predetermined quantitative or qualitative boundaries which, when reached or exceeded, trigger specific safety responses, interventions, or escalations

A human-made construct in safety management and risk engineering: the systematic application of measures to reduce, transfer, or eliminate the impact of threats. Risk-control encompasses policies, procedures, technical safeguards, and organizational practices designed to keep risk within acceptable levels. It is built to persist through institutional knowledge, documented standards, and repeatable processes.

A human-made safety practice that identifies and eliminates the root causes of potential nonconformities before they occur — distinct from corrective-action which addresses actual problems already present. Built on risk assessment, hazard analysis, and systematic review processes.

A human-made safety practice consisting of deliberate actions taken to reduce, control, or eliminate hazards and prevent incidents. It is designed, planned, and implemented through organizational procedures — not spontaneous reaction but a structured approach to managing risk in workplaces and systems.

A human-made mistake-proofing mechanism — a device or process design that prevents errors from occurring or makes them immediately obvious. Originated in the Toyota Production System as a way to build quality into processes by making it impossible or extremely difficult to make a particular type of error.

Error-prevention is a human-made discipline of designing processes, systems, and environments to stop human and organizational errors from occurring in the first place. It encompasses techniques, protocols, and institutional practices built through centuries of learning from accidents and near-misses. The concept persists through safety engineering standards, training programs, quality management systems, and the accumulated body of safety science that organizations deploy proactively to eliminate error pathways before harm can occur.

A human-made framework for iterative project management and product development, structured around time-boxed sprints, defined roles (product owner, scrum master, development team), and regular ceremonies (planning, daily stand-up, review, retrospective) designed to deliver working increments of a product through empirical process control and self-organizing teams.

A specific, measurable target set within a safety management system to reduce risk or improve safety performance. Objectives are defined through risk assessment, aligned with the organization's safety policy, and tracked through indicators. Examples include reducing incident rates, achieving compliance milestones, or implementing new safety protocols by a target date.

A human-made role and institution dedicated to designing and delivering safety training to workers and organizations. Safety trainers develop curricula, conduct instruction sessions, assess trainee competency, and maintain training records. The role exists as a formal position within occupational health and safety management systems, distinguishing it from informal peer mentoring by requiring structured pedagogical methods and documented competence evaluation.

A human-made practice of delivering a brief safety-focused talk or reminder at the start of meetings, workshops, or shifts — a structured institutional habit built to persist workplace safety awareness through repeated daily ritual.

An indicator is a human-made sign, metric, or signal deliberately designed to convey information about the state of a system. It is a structured representation that stands in for something else, enabling monitoring, assessment, and decision-making. Indicators are human artifacts — they do not exist in nature but are constructed through convention, measurement, and interpretation, and they persist through language, notation, and institutional practice.

A constraint in a system that limits overall throughput — the narrowest point through which flow must pass. Human-made concept used in operations research, manufacturing (Theory of Constraints), software engineering, and systems thinking to identify and manage limiting factors.

A demonstrated ability — the proven combination of knowledge, skill, and judgment that enables effective performance in a specific domain. Human-made concept used in safety management, professional certification, and organizational capability assessment.

A quantifiable measure of safety performance that is designated as critical for organizational safety success — a key performance indicator specifically for tracking and evaluating safety outcomes, processes, and leading indicators.

A human-made analytical construct in safety management: an observable indicator — such as a near-miss, weak signal, or early warning sign — that a safety failure or incident may be imminent. It is a categorized concept built into safety reporting systems and risk assessment frameworks, persisted through organizational practice, training, and documentation.

A human-made signaling construct: a system or mechanism designed to provide advance notice of an impending event or danger. Built to persist through standardized alert protocols, communication channels, and early-detection infrastructure across safety management, meteorology, finance, and other risk-monitoring domains.

A structured framework of procedures, roles, and processes that an organization establishes to manage safety — human-made, designed to prevent harm, control risks, and ensure compliance through organized systems rather than ad hoc measures

A human-made systematic set of documented steps and protocols that an organization establishes to ensure tasks are performed in a way that prevents harm, controls risk, and maintains compliance. Designed to persist through written documentation, training programs, and institutional memory.

A human-made construct representing the structured knowledge, skills, abilities, and behaviors that an organization develops, maintains, and assesses in its personnel to enable safe performance of work. It is institutionalized through training programs, competency frameworks, assessment protocols, and credentialing systems that ensure workers can identify hazards, apply controls, and respond to emergencies. The construct persists through organizational HR processes, competency matrices, and regulatory compliance requirements that tie individual capability to operational safety.

Safety-momentum is a human-made organizational concept: the accumulated state of safety efforts, incidents, and interventions that shapes current safety performance. It is built to persist through documented practices, institutional memory, and cultural norms — a construct designed to capture the idea that safety performance is not random but carries the weight of past actions.

A human-made safety management document: a systematic register of identified hazards, their assessed risk levels, assigned control measures, responsible persons, and review status. Built to persist through organizational record-keeping practices and safety database systems.

A human-made organizational practice: designated periods or standing assignments where individuals monitor operations specifically for emerging safety conditions, distinct from formal inspections by virtue of its continuous, attentive posture rather than checklist-driven verification. Built to persist through shift protocols, peer-observation programs, and safety-standing assignments that maintain organizational vigilance as a sustained habit rather than an episodic activity.

A lagging-indicator is a human-made measurement construct — a retrospective metric that quantifies outcomes after they have occurred. It serves as a backward-looking signal in performance evaluation systems, recording what actually happened rather than what is expected to happen.

A human-made institutional construct — structured recognition and incentives designed to reinforce positive safety behaviors, attitudes, and outcomes within organizations. Built to persist through formal programs, policies, and cultural practices that shape safety culture.

Human-made system of recommended practices and behavioral norms that guide workplace safety decisions without the force of mandatory standards. Built to persist through documentation, training materials, and organizational culture that shape daily safety choices.

Human-made reference point or standard against which safety performance, practices, or systems are measured — derived from industry standards, best practices, regulatory requirements, or peer comparisons. Built to persist through published standards, rating frameworks, and comparative reporting mechanisms.

Human-made system of indicators, alerts, and early warning signals that organizations use to detect emerging safety issues before they escalate into incidents. Built to persist through monitoring frameworks, reporting channels, and communication protocols.

Human-made pattern-recognition construct used in safety engineering and analysis to identify characteristic configurations of indicators, behaviors, and conditions that signal a particular type of risk profile or safety state. Built to persist through incident databases, safety training curricula, and organizational knowledge systems that encode pattern recognition across teams and generations.

A human-made assessment construct that captures the state of safety conditions, compliance levels, and risk exposures at a specific point in time — built to persist through documentation, dashboards, and reporting systems that organizations use to track safety posture across shifts, periods, and audits.

A human-made behavioral prompt or cue designed to reinforce safety practices at the point of action — built to persist through signage, checklists, digital alerts, and verbal prompts that keep safety top-of-mind during work execution.

A human-made practice of systematically assessing safety performance against defined criteria and benchmarks. Built to persist through documented review cycles, audit trails, and institutionalized assessment routines that organizations maintain to ensure ongoing safety improvement.

A human-made structured review process conducted after an event, operation, or incident to extract lessons, identify what went well and what did not, and convert experience into organizational learning. Built to persist through documented minutes, action items, and follow-up tracking that close the loop between observation and change.

A human-made mechanism or system (software, process, or institutional arrangement) designed to record, aggregate, and maintain safety-related data, incidents, metrics, and observations over time, enabling longitudinal analysis and trend detection

A human-made risk-mitigation framework that ranks control measures by effectiveness: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment. Built to persist through safety standards, training, and regulatory practice.

A human-made governance construct through which an organization declares the types and amounts of risk it is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives, distinguishing tolerated risk from unacceptable risk.

A human-made procedural construct that establishes the conditions, authority, and process for halting an activity, process, or system when safety is at risk — the deliberate pause of operations to prevent harm.

A human-made systematic method of walking through work areas to observe safety conditions, engage workers about hazards, and identify risks proactively before incidents occur. It is a structured observational practice maintained as part of organizational safety programs, distinct from checklist-driven inspections by its emphasis on dialogue and situational awareness.

A human-made organizational construct referring to the capabilities, competencies, resources, and infrastructure that an entity develops and maintains to perform safety management effectively. It encompasses trained personnel, available tools, established procedures, and organizational readiness — all deliberately cultivated rather than naturally occurring.

A human-made construct referring to the systematic recording, storage, and management of safety-related information within an organization. It includes incident reports, safety procedures, training records, audit findings, and regulatory compliance documents — deliberately created and maintained to support safety management, risk communication, and organizational learning.

A human-made institutional construct: the formal declaration by organizational leadership that safety is a core value equal to or above production targets, communicated through policy documents, resource allocation, and visible actions. It establishes the tone from the top that cascades through all safety systems.

A human-made organizational construct — the systematic practice and institutional commitment to anticipating, identifying, and eliminating hazards before they cause harm. It is built to persist through procedures, rules, training, and monitoring systems that shape organizational behavior toward harm-avoidance.

A human-made organizational construct — the categorization and recording of events that had the potential to cause harm but did not, because of chance or timely intervention. Built to persist through incident-reporting systems, safety databases, and organizational learning processes so that latent failures can be identified before they cause actual harm.

A safety-signal is a human-made indicator designed to communicate the presence, status, or absence of a safety condition through standardized sensory cues. It persists through institutional standardization and regulatory codification — established by safety authorities, enforced via compliance, and sustained through training and awareness programs.

A human-made systematic error in safety judgment — the tendency to overweight readily available, vivid, or emotionally salient hazards while underweighting statistically more significant but less visible risks. It persists through institutional decision-making, risk assessment protocols, and resource allocation patterns.

A human-made construct for the organized knowledge, skills, abilities, and attitudes that individuals and organizations develop to identify hazards, manage risks, and sustain safe operations. It persists through formal training curricula, certification programs, competency assessments, and organizational development practices — all human-designed mechanisms for building and verifying safety-related capability.

A human-made construct for the planned time or operational spacing between scheduled safety activities — inspections, audits, drills, or reviews. It persists through policy documents, regulatory requirements, and organizational procedure, providing a measurable cadence that ensures safety systems are periodically exercised and validated.

A human-made systematic examination and evaluation of safety-related activities, procedures, documentation, and performance against established standards, regulations, or organizational policies. It persists through audit programs, checklists, reports, findings, and corrective-action tracking maintained by auditors, compliance teams, and regulatory bodies.

A human-made system of signals, alarms, signs, or communications designed to alert people to potential hazards or unsafe conditions. Built to persist through institutional practice, regulatory requirement, and technological deployment.

A human-made body of information, data, and documentation created through observation, measurement, and recording to support or undermine safety-related claims, decisions, and practices. Built to persist through institutional record-keeping, regulatory requirements, and evidentiary standards.

A human-made financial allocation mechanism: the planned earmarking of organizational funds specifically for safety programs, equipment, training, and compliance activities. Built to persist through fiscal planning cycles, budgetary procedures, and regulatory mandates that require dedicated resourcing for safety.

A human-made business model: offering a basic product or service at zero cost while charging for premium features or enhanced access. Built to persist through network effects — free users expand the user base and attract paying users, while the pricing tier captures value from power users.

A human-made organizational construct: the shared disposition toward safety values, priorities, and behaviors within a group or institution. Built to persist through leadership signaling, training reinforcement, reward structures, and collective habit — measurable through surveys and observable in workplace decisions.

A human-made financial institution: a mechanism for pooling small voluntary contributions from many individuals to fund specific projects, ventures, or causes, typically facilitated through dedicated online platforms. Built to persist through platform infrastructure, social proof mechanisms, and reward/equity structures that align contributor incentives with project success.

A human-made organizational and technological mechanism: the practice of obtaining services, ideas, or content by soliciting contributions from a large group of people, especially from an online community, rather than from traditional employees or suppliers. Built to persist through digital platforms that match contributors with requesters, reputation systems that quality-assure output, and network effects that make the model self-reinforcing.

A human-made institutional construct: a formally constituted body — typically governmental or independent regulatory — established by legislation or mandate to oversee, develop, and enforce safety standards across one or more domains. Built to persist through statutory authority, institutional memory, and ongoing regulatory enforcement.

A human-made behavioral construct: the practice and discipline of observing, abiding by, and conforming to safety rules, standards, and procedures within an organization or system. It is the norm-based side of compliance — not the enforcement mechanism itself, but the ongoing practice of adherence.

A human-made institutional-technical construct: self-executing agreements encoded as computer programs that automatically enforce and execute contractual terms when predefined conditions are met. Built to persist through cryptographic recording on distributed ledgers and automated by consensus protocols.

A human-made organizational construct: the active participation and involvement of individuals and groups in safety-related activities — volunteering ideas, attending safety meetings, participating in inspections and committees, going beyond mere compliance to contribute proactively to workplace safety.

A human-made institutional-legal construct: a model of collaborative development and distribution where creators grant others the rights to use, modify, and share their work under published licenses. Built to persist through legal frameworks (copyright licenses such as GPL, MIT, Apache), community norms of reciprocity, and distribution platforms.

A human-made framework for how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value. It specifies the value proposition, target customers, revenue streams, cost structure, and key resources and activities — a structured way of describing how a venture is designed to be economically sustainable.

A human-made construct: a measurable signal derived from proactive activities and conditions that predict future outcomes or performance, enabling anticipatory intervention rather than retrospective assessment.

A human-made organizational practice: granting workers the authority, resources, and obligation to stop work, address hazards, and influence safety decisions without fear of reprisal. It is built by policy, reinforced by culture, and sustained through training and leadership modeling.

A human-made fiduciary role and practice: the responsibility assumed by individuals or groups to care for, maintain, and improve the safety conditions of a workplace, system, or community — extending beyond one's own immediate duties to look after the collective safety of all who are affected.

A human-made institutional construct: a structured set of guidelines, standards, procedures, and controls designed to govern, direct, and regulate the operations of an organization. It is built to persist through formal adoption (e.g. COBIT, NIST CSF, ISO 27001) and provides a repeatable mechanism for aligning actions with objectives, managing risk, and ensuring compliance.

Data-ethics is a human-made field of study and practice concerned with the moral principles governing the collection, processing, storage, and use of data. Built to persist through professional codes of conduct, regulatory frameworks, academic disciplines, and institutional review boards.

A safety bottleneck is a human-made constraining factor within a safety system — a limited resource, procedural gap, or organizational weakness that caps overall safety performance regardless of strengths elsewhere. Built to persist through risk assessments, bottleneck analyses, and corrective action programs.

A safety feedback loop is a human-made mechanism within organizational safety systems that channels information from incidents, audits, and observations back into design, training, and procedural updates. Built to persist through documented learning cycles, safety bulletins, and continuous improvement frameworks.

A human-made systematic process that identifies, implements, and sustains changes to enhance safety performance in organizations. Built to persist through structured methodologies, measurement cycles, and organizational learning mechanisms.

A human-made institutional mechanism — legal, regulatory, and organizational — that protects individuals who report wrongdoing, illegality, or safety violations from retaliation. Built to persist through codified protections, anonymous reporting channels, and enforcement procedures.

The institutional practice of delegating decision authority to algorithmic systems — software, rulesets, and statistical models — that process inputs and produce decisions affecting individuals, groups, or organizations without direct human intervention at the point of decision. Human-made as concept, practice, and infrastructure: credit scoring, hiring screens, content moderation, benefits eligibility, diagnostic triage.

A pre-structured text format with placeholders and instructions for generating AI system inputs — a reusable artifact built through deliberate design, versioning, and iteration, persisting through templates repositories and shared collections.

A practice and set of techniques for making the inner workings of automated systems — especially machine learning models and algorithmic decision processes — visible, interpretable, and understandable to humans. Persists through documentation, auditing frameworks, and standardized reporting protocols like model cards and algorithmic impact assessments.

A human-made governance practice that assigns responsibility for the outcomes of automated systems to the organizations and individuals that design, deploy, and operate them. Built to persist as a legal and ethical requirement for AI governance, regulation, and engineering accountability.

A human-made practice through which organizations systematically accumulate, retain, and apply knowledge from experience to improve operations and outcomes. Built to persist through documented processes, shared routines, and institutional memory mechanisms.

A human-made examination procedure that systematically evaluates automated systems for compliance with legal, ethical, and organizational standards. Built to persist through formal audit frameworks, documented findings, and regulatory reporting mechanisms.
A human-made metric that measures past safety performance through recorded incidents, injuries, and failures. Built to persist through safety reporting systems and regulatory records.

A human-made control concept: a regulation mechanism that uses information about inputs or anticipated disturbances to adjust a system before an error occurs, rather than reacting to output deviations after the fact. Built to persist through engineering design, process control, and organizational management practice.

A human-made practice of using statistical methods, historical incident data, leading indicators, and predictive models to anticipate future safety performance and identify potential hazards before they materialize — institutionalized through safety planning, risk assessment protocols, and predictive analytics systems maintained by organizations.

A human-made practice of systematically evaluating safety systems, controls, and performance against established standards, regulations, and benchmarks to produce structured findings that drive safety improvement.

A best-practice is a human-made concept: a method, technique, or process that has been empirically shown to produce superior results and is formally adopted as the standard within an organization or discipline. It persists through documentation, teaching, and institutional memory — not as a natural property of the method but as a socially recognized benchmark of excellence.

A control tower is a human-made governance mechanism: a centralized monitoring and coordination function that collects data from distributed operations, analyzes performance against targets, and directs corrective action. Originally built as an aviation concept, it has been institutionalized across enterprise management, supply chains, safety systems, and project governance as a dedicated function for real-time situational awareness and command authority.

A human-made analytical method for understanding how artificial intelligence models produce their outputs — techniques, frameworks, and procedures that make model decision processes transparent and understandable to humans, built to persist through documentation, code, and training

A human-made reasoning technique in which an agent is guided to express intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final conclusion. Used in education, problem-solving, and AI prompting to improve accuracy and transparency of complex inference.

The accumulated information, practices, and understanding about safety that an organization collects, maintains, and applies to prevent harm and respond to incidents. It is human-made through documentation, training, incident analysis, and experience sharing.
A structured mechanism allowing workers, contractors, or stakeholders to report safety concerns, observations, or improvement ideas to those responsible for managing organizational risks.

A human-made classification framework that ranks risk control measures by their effectiveness at reducing hazard exposure — from elimination and substitution through engineering, administrative controls, to personal protective equipment. Built as a decision tool for safety professionals to prioritize interventions, it persists through standards (OSHA, ISO 45001), training curricula, and regulatory compliance documentation.

A human-made document produced by structured safety audits — it records findings, non-conformances, observations, and recommended corrective actions. The report persists through formal documentation systems, regulatory requirements, and organizational record-keeping practices. It is a tool for translating audit observations into actionable safety-management input.

A human-made system of planned and reactive activities to preserve and restore the functionality of safety-critical equipment, procedures, and organizational structures. It persists through documented schedules, checklists, and records that ensure safety systems continue to operate as designed over time.

A human-made organizational practice of deliberately advancing safety values, priorities, and behaviors through communication, recognition, and cultural initiatives. It persists through campaigns, leadership messaging, and reward systems that sustain attention to safety beyond compliance requirements.
A human-made specific action or method performed or sustained to advance safety outcomes. It persists through training, routine, and institutional reinforcement.
A human-made metric or indicator system used to gauge the state of safety within an organization or system — a construct built to make safety conditions visible and comparable across time.

A human-made strategic plan that sets the direction, priorities, and approach for achieving and maintaining safety within an organization or system — a construct designed to coordinate all safety-related activities toward common objectives.

A human-made systematic process for identifying hazards, evaluating the likelihood and severity of potential harm, and determining controls to mitigate those risks. Built on formal methodologies, standards, and documentation that persist through institutional practice and regulatory frameworks.

The constructed concept of shared group belief that the environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — including speaking up, admitting errors, proposing novel ideas, or asking questions without fear of humiliation or retaliation. Coined by Robert Weiss and developed by Amy Edmondson as a measurable organizational construct, not the natural feeling of safety itself.

An organizational framework for handling incidents that categorizes behaviors into three types — honest human error (addressed through system improvement), at-risk behavior (addressed through coaching), and reckless behavior (addressed through discipline) — balancing accountability with learning

A human-made construct of organizational theory and crisis management: the structured capacity of institutions to absorb disruption, adapt under stress, and recover while maintaining core functions — deliberately designed through redundancy, modularity, and learning mechanisms

A human-made organizational practice: the structured process by which workers and members of an institution document, escalate, and communicate information about accidents, near-misses, hazards, and safety violations. Built to persist through forms, channels, and institutional memory so that incident data feeds learning and corrective action.

A human-made organizational practice: scheduled, recurring activities designed to maintain or improve safety performance within an institution. Includes pre-shift safety briefings, scheduled safety walks, routine equipment inspections, and periodic drills — systematic repetitions that embed safety into daily operations rather than leaving them to ad hoc response.
A human-made organizational practice: the process of creating systems and procedures to ensure an organization can continue operating during and after a disruption or disaster.

A human-made organizational practice: a structured process by which an organization evaluates its own safety posture, controls, and compliance against established standards and objectives. Built to persist through documented procedures, recurring assessment cycles, and institutional memory in safety records.

A human-made conceptual structure: an organized set of categories, relationships, and principles that shapes how information is processed, understood, and retrieved. Built to persist through documentation, teaching, and repeated application in problem-solving.

A human-made visual representation of information, data, or knowledge designed to present complex information quickly and clearly through the integration of graphical elements, minimal text, and visual design. Built to persist through digital media and print as a means of rapid knowledge transmission.

A human-made cognitive technique for structuring perception and communication by selecting and highlighting certain aspects of a situation to promote a particular interpretation, evaluation, or course of action. Built through discourse, media, education, and social reinforcement to persist across contexts.

A structured simulated emergency exercise in which participants practice evacuation routes, response actions, and communication procedures under conditions that replicate a real fire event. Created and sustained by institutional training programs, regulatory mandates, and organizational safety protocols to build muscle memory and test infrastructure readiness.

A taxonomy of the distinct ways a system, process, or component can fail — human-engineered for safety analysis, risk assessment, and resilience planning. Built to persist through failure-mode-and-effects-analysis (FMEA), fault-tree analysis, and incident post-mortems, providing structured vocabulary for diagnosing breakdowns.

The concept of how individuals and organizations identify, interpret, and prioritize safety-related signals — a cognitive-institutional map that shapes what hazards are noticed, how they are rated, and what actions they trigger.

A rug plot is a human-made data visualization technique that displays individual data points as small tick marks along a single axis, providing a raw view of data density and distribution without binning. It is built to persist through software libraries and printed statistical reports, serving as a complement to histograms and kernel density estimates by showing every observation without aggregation.

A creed is a human-made, systematically formulated statement of core beliefs and principles, authored for the purpose of defining group identity, guiding conduct, and enabling collective identification. It persists through codification — written text, oral recitation, and institutional teaching — and functions as a boundary marker between those who hold it and those who do not.

A pictogram is a human-made symbolic representation that uses pictures, icons, or simplified drawings to convey information, instructions, or concepts independent of language. Law 1: this is a human-made communication convention. Law 2a: the pictogram is the map (the symbolic system), not any natural image.

A stem-and-leaf plot is a human-made data display technique that organizes quantitative data by splitting each value into a stem (leading digit(s)) and a leaf (trailing digit), arranging the stems in order and listing leaves beside them to show the distribution while preserving the original data values.

A human-made data visualization that maps quantitative or positional data onto a polar coordinate system aligned with the sun's path — showing solar position, insolation, shadow casting, or seasonal light patterns. Used in architectural design, agricultural planning, and renewable energy siting to visualize how sunlight interacts with terrain, buildings, or land over the course of a day or year.

A human-made organization or format for storing, arranging, and accessing collections of information so that operations on that information can be performed efficiently. Built to persist as a defined arrangement of data elements with specified relationships and access operations, implemented in software, algorithms, or documentation.

A human-made communicative construct: the practice of framing safety-related information — incidents, near-misses, procedures, risks — as stories or narratives within an organization. Built to persist through organizational memory, training materials, safety briefings, and culture-shaping discourse.

A human-made construct — a structured set of interconnected beliefs, values, and worldviews held by an individual or group, organized and sustained through teaching, ritual, language, and social practice to provide meaning, identity, and behavioral guidance.

A structured organizational practice in which personnel who have mastered safety protocols, hazard recognition, and risk management are certified to deliver safety training to their peers — creating a multiplier effect for safety culture and compliance through pedagogical cascade rather than centralized instruction.

A human-made verification practice that validates a result by comparing it against an independently derived or computed value — built to persist as a method of quality assurance in engineering, science, and everyday reasoning.

A statistical method in which the dataset is partitioned into complementary subsets, the model is trained on one subset and validated on the other, to assess generalization performance and prevent overfitting. Human-made, built to persist through mathematical practice and empirical validation.

A human-made sequence of data processing steps where the output of each step feeds into the input of the next, orchestrated by code or configuration to move and transform data from source to destination.

A human-made visual representation method where multiple quantitative variables are displayed as vertices in parallel, connected by lines so that each line represents a single data point across all dimensions

A human-made thematic map that divides geographic regions into zones and color-codes each zone according to a statistical variable, enabling visual comparison of region-level data such as density, income, or election results across a mapped territory

A human-made visual encoding method that displays individual data points along a single axis, typically used to show the distribution of a single variable. Each point represents one observation, and the density of points reveals the underlying distribution. Built to persist as a standard method in statistical graphics.

A human-made continuous vector representation of discrete data (words, images, entities) in a high-dimensional space, designed so that semantic similarity is reflected as geometric proximity. Built to persist through training pipelines and deployed in retrieval, classification, and generation systems.

A human-made data summarization tool that aggregates, cross-tabulates, and restructures tabular data by grouping rows along specified dimension fields and computing aggregate functions (count, sum, average, etc.) on measure fields, enabling multi-dimensional exploration of structured datasets.

A human-made notation for describing algorithms in structured natural language rather than a programming language, using English-like statements, indentation, and control-flow keywords to specify logic without syntax constraints.

A human-made statistical concept describing how often different values occur within a dataset. It is a mapping or table of value ranges to their observed or expected counts — a framework invented by statisticians to organize and analyze empirical data.

A human-made data visualization technique that displays comparisons across categories using bars grouped side-by-side for each category value. Each group contains separate bars for subcategories, enabling direct comparison within and between groups. It persists through charting libraries, spreadsheet software, and data analysis tools as a standard visualization pattern.

The phenomenon in machine learning and statistics where the statistical properties of the target variable or input data change over time, causing a model trained on older data to degrade in predictive performance. It is human-made, designed as a diagnostic concept in model operations, and persists through the practice of data science, MLOps tooling, and sustained research into non-stationary learning environments.

A human-made statistical concept identifying data points that deviate markedly from the pattern of a dataset. Defined by formal criteria — distance from quartiles, z-score thresholds, or model residuals — the concept persists through statistical education, data-analysis practice, and the institutions that standardize anomaly detection.

A tabular construct used in statistics and machine learning to summarize classification performance by organizing prediction outcomes into four cells: true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, enabling derivation of accuracy, precision, recall, and related metrics.

A slope graph is a human-made data visualization technique that displays comparisons between two or more states (typically start and end) across discrete categories using simple straight lines connecting the values. Designed by human chart designers to make directional change legible at a glance, it persists through visual design conventions and published examples in data communication practice.

An iterative optimization algorithm that minimizes a differentiable objective function by repeatedly stepping in the direction of steepest descent of the gradient, parameterized by step size and convergence criteria, persisted through mathematical formalism and software implementation.

A human-made statistical visualization that displays all individual data points as non-overlapping symbols arranged to show the underlying distribution — like seeds in a beehive — preserving every observation while avoiding the information loss of binned charts like histograms.

A human-made diagnostic visualization that plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate for a binary classifier across all decision thresholds, enabling operating-point selection that balances sensitivity and specificity.

A human-made data visualization technique: a circular chart divided into sectors where each sector's radius encodes a value, derived from Florence Nightingale's military mortality diagrams to display proportional data in polar form.

A statistical method for modeling the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables, built on mathematical formalism that persists through computation, teaching, and applied practice across every domain that quantifies cause and effect.

A mathematical function or table that assigns probabilities to each possible outcome of a random variable. It is human-made formalism that persists through mathematical notation, computation, and teaching.

An ensemble machine learning method that constructs a multitude of decision trees at training time and outputs the class that is the mode of the classes (classification) or mean prediction (regression) of the individual trees. It is a human-made algorithm that persists through software libraries, academic literature, and computational practice.

A machine learning paradigm where models are trained on labeled data — input-output pairs — to learn a mapping function that generalizes to unseen inputs. Human-made to enable systems that acquire knowledge through examples with known correct answers, enabling prediction and classification.
A human-made analytical technique for extracting patterns from data, systematized through mathematical formalism and peer-reviewed practice in the discipline of statistics.

A human-made statistical technique where sample datasets are repeatedly drawn from a larger dataset or its empirical distribution, using methods such as bootstrapping, jackknife, and permutation testing. Built to persist through standardized practice in statistical inference and machine learning evaluation.

A human-made statistical control method for managing the expected proportion of incorrect rejections among all rejections in multiple hypothesis testing. It is a decision-theoretic construct developed to address the problem of false positives when conducting many simultaneous tests, operationalized through the q-value andBH procedure.

A human-made statistical procedure for adjusting significance thresholds when conducting multiple simultaneous hypothesis tests, preventing the inflation of false discovery rates. Implemented via methods including Bonferroni correction, Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, and Holm-Bonferroni method. Persists through statistical software, textbook pedagogy, and standard practice in genomics and data science.

A human-made mathematical model specifying a continuous probability distribution defined by a bell-shaped curve characterized by its mean and standard deviation. Built to persist through formal notation, tables, and computational libraries for statistical inference.

A human-made statistical function that estimates the cumulative distribution of a random variable from observed data points. Built to persist as a mathematical construct through formal specification and algorithmic computation.

A visualization method used in binary classification evaluation: a two-dimensional plot tracing the tradeoff between precision and recall as the decision threshold of a classifier varies, with each point on the curve corresponding to a specific threshold value.

A non-parametric method for estimating the probability density function of a random variable by placing a kernel (smooth, symmetric function such as a Gaussian) at each data point and summing the contributions. Human-made as a mathematical algorithm designed to persist through computation, teaching, and application across statistics, data science, and machine learning.

A correlation matrix is a human-made data structure that encodes the pairwise correlation coefficients between a set of variables. It is a square, symmetric matrix whose entries quantify linear relationships between variables. Built to persist through mathematical formalism, statistical software, and scientific data analysis practice.

Logistic regression is a human-made statistical method for modeling the probability of a binary outcome. It maps predictor variables to a probability space through the logistic (sigmoid) function. Created as a mathematical tool and sustained through software libraries, textbooks, and data-science practice, it persists as a formalized procedure for classification and probability estimation.

A human-made ensemble machine learning method that builds models sequentially, where each new model corrects the residual errors of the combined previous models by fitting to the negative gradient of the loss function. Persisted through software implementations (XGBoost, LightGBM), mathematical formalism, and pedagogical use in predictive modeling.

A human-made statistical measure that quantifies the linear relationship between two variables while controlling for the effect of one or more additional variables. It is constructed through regression-based residualization or inverse covariance computation, and persists through statistical software packages, econometric practice, and scientific methodology.

a human-made analytical technique in statistics and machine learning that examines the differences between observed and predicted values, diagnosing model fit and identifying systematic errors in predictive models

A human-made dimensionality reduction technique that transforms correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated principal components via eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix or SVD of the data matrix

A human-made method of organizing and representing data points ordered sequentially by time, used to study temporal patterns, trends, and dynamics across scientific, economic, and engineering disciplines.

A human-made statistical and machine learning technique for partitioning a dataset into groups (clusters) such that intra-group similarity is maximized and inter-group similarity is minimized, used for pattern discovery and exploratory data analysis.
A human-made visualization construct that maps predicted values against observed outcomes to assess model reliability

A statistical construct that represents the distribution of observed data values from a sample or experiment. It organizes actual measurements or observations into a frequency pattern, serving as the observable counterpart to theoretical probability distributions. Persisted through mathematical notation, statistical tables, and computational algorithms that summarize observed data.

a data visualization display that arranges a grid of scatter plots showing pairwise relationships between variables in a dataset, enabling comparative pattern reading across all variable pairs in a single view

A human-made analytical construct in machine learning and statistics — a diagnostic visualization that tracks model performance against training effort to reveal learning trajectories and inform data acquisition decisions.

A human-made statistical visualization: a scatter plot used in meta-analysis that displays study-specific treatment effects against a measure of their precision (typically standard error or sample size), with a funnel-shaped confidence interval to visually assess publication bias and small-study effects.

A human-made statistical visualization: a scatter plot used in regression diagnostics that displays residuals (prediction errors) on the vertical axis against predicted values or independent variables on the horizontal axis, enabling visual assessment of model fit, heteroscedasticity, and nonlinearity.

A human-made data preprocessing practice in machine learning: transforming raw variables into informative features that better capture the underlying relationship with the target variable, improving model performance through domain knowledge and statistical techniques.

A human-made statistical visualization: a scatter plot matrix augmented with box plots along each marginal axis, showing both pairwise variable relationships and univariate distributions simultaneously in a single composite plot.

A human-made data infrastructure component: a centralized system for storing, managing, and serving features (derived variables) used by machine learning models across training and inference. Built to persist through software deployment pipelines and shared across model teams.

A matrix-based data visualization that shows set intersections through a grid of dots combined with bar charts, designed to scale to many more sets than Venn diagrams allow. Built by humans in computational set theory and information visualization to make large intersection structures readable where Venn diagrams fail.

A measure or ranking that quantifies how much each input feature contributes to a model's predictive performance — a construct built by data scientists to interpret and explain machine learning model behavior.

A method for assessing the importance of features in a machine learning model by randomly shuffling the values of a single feature and measuring the resulting degradation in model performance — a human-made computational procedure for feature evaluation.

A human-made scatter plot showing the within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) against the number of clusters K, used to identify the optimal K where the rate of decrease sharply shifts — built to persist as a model selection heuristic in clustering.

A human-made data visualization that shows two quantitative variables as a series of dots connected by sloped lines, where each dot represents a value on one axis and the line connecting consecutive dots encodes the change between them — built to persist in statistical and scientific communication as an alternative to line charts for sparse data

A human-made interpretability method in machine learning that computes Shapley values from cooperative game theory to assign each feature an additive contribution to a model's prediction for a given instance — built to persist as the standard for locally faithful feature attribution

A human-made machine learning procedure for selecting a subset of relevant features from a feature set, designed to reduce dimensionality, improve model performance, and increase interpretability through systematic evaluation strategies

Feature extraction is the human-made process of identifying and selecting relevant characteristics or patterns from raw data, transforming it into a representation suitable for analysis or modeling. It is a systematic procedure — whether manual, algorithmic, or hybrid — that distills raw observations into structured signals humans can work with.

Influence plot is a human-made statistical visualization that displays data points' leverage and influence on regression or other model fits — typically combining fitted values, residuals, and influence measures like Cook's distance or DFFITS into a single diagnostic plot so analysts can identify outliers and high-leverage observations that disproportionately affect model estimates.

A human-made statistical visualization that maps the marginal relationship between a single feature and a model's predicted outcome by computing average predictions across a grid of feature values, holding all other features at their observed or baseline values. It persists as a diagnostic practice in machine learning interpretability.

A human-made statistical procedure for hypothesis testing that constructs the null distribution by randomly shuffling observed data labels, enabling exact p-value calculation without parametric assumptions about the underlying population.

A human-made statistical visualization used in predictive modeling and marketing analytics that shows how much better a model's predictions are compared to random guessing, plotting the cumulative percentage of positive responses captured (lift) against the percentage of the population contacted at successive scoring thresholds.

A methodological practice in machine learning where a dataset is partitioned into two subsets — one for training a model and one for evaluating its generalization performance. Human-made because it is an invented convention for measuring model reliability, encoded in software libraries and taught as standard practice in data science. It persists through code implementations, documentation, and the institutionalized norms of the field.
A human-made process for breaking text into smaller units called tokens, each carrying semantic or syntactic significance for computational processing.
A human-made technique for artificially expanding training datasets by applying controlled transformations that preserve the underlying label or meaning, designed to improve model generalization.

A statistical method for fitting a smooth curve to scattered data points by minimizing a weighted sum of squares subject to a smoothness penalty. It extends cubic splines by adding a tuning parameter that controls the trade-off between fidelity to the data and smoothness of the fit.

A human-made analytical practice for investigating datasets to discover patterns, spot anomalies, test hypotheses, and check assumptions — primarily through summary statistics and visualizations. Coined by John Tukey in 1977, it persists through taught methodology, published literature, and standard practice in statistics and data science workflows.

A human-made tabular construct that organizes pairwise covariances between variables in a dataset, encoding the joint variability structure so that correlations, variances, and principal axes can be computed

A visualization technique used to assess the accuracy of predicted probabilities from classification models: plots predicted probability bins on the x-axis against the observed frequency of positive outcomes on the y-axis, enabling diagnosis of model overconfidence or underconfidence.

A proper scoring rule for evaluating the accuracy of probabilistic predictions: it computes the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual binary outcomes. Created by meteorologist Glenn Brier in 1950 for weather forecasting, it persists as a standard metric in classification model evaluation, embedded in statistical software packages and taught in machine learning curricula.

Data leakage is a machine learning failure mode where information from outside the training scope — such as test set data, future information, or target variable correlates — inadvertently enters the training process. It produces overoptimistic performance estimates and is prevented through careful data partitioning, proper preprocessing order, and temporal validation protocols. It persists through methodological documentation, validation frameworks, and teaching practices in data science.

A validation set is a human-made partition of data held out from training to provide an independent estimate of model performance during development. It is used for hyperparameter selection, early stopping, and model comparison without contaminating the test set. It persists through experimental design conventions and machine learning software frameworks that split datasets into train, validation, and test subsets.

A residual is the difference between an observed value and the value predicted by a statistical model or regression. It is a human-made diagnostic quantity used to assess model fit, detect outliers, and verify assumptions about error structure. Built to persist through documentation, software libraries, and scientific practice.

A scoring rule is a human-made evaluation metric that assigns a numerical score to the accuracy of probabilistic predictions, quantifying how well predicted probability distributions match observed outcomes. It formalizes the assessment of forecast quality through mathematically defined functions that reward calibrated, sharp probabilistic statements and penalize miscalibration and imprecision.

A human-made epistemic tool that produces quantified uncertainty about future outcomes — predicted probability distributions or point probabilities assigned to events. It persists through formal methods (Bayesian inference, statistical modeling, ensemble methods) and is taught, published, and operationalized across disciplines (meteorology, epidemiology, economics, machine learning).

A human-made concept in machine learning methodology describing the unintended information flow from training data into model evaluation, violating the boundary between training and testing phases. It persists through shared terminology in ML literature and practice, as a failure mode that practitioners must actively prevent.

A human-made mathematical function that quantifies the discrepancy between a model's predictions and actual target values, producing a single scalar measure used to guide optimization of model parameters during training.

A human-made concept in machine learning describing configuration variables whose values are set by a practitioner before the training process begins — as opposed to parameters learned during training. Examples include learning rate, number of hidden layers, regularization strength, and batch size. The concept exists as a design choice space that practitioners navigate to optimize model performance.

A human-made concept in machine learning describing the tension between two sources of error that determine prediction quality: bias (error from erroneous assumptions in the learning algorithm, leading to underfitting) and variance (error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in the training set, leading to overfitting). The tradeoff is the principle that minimizing total error requires balancing these two conflicting objectives — reducing bias tends to increase variance and vice versa.

A visual encoding is a human-made mapping system that translates data attributes into visual properties such as position, color, size, and shape. It is a conceptual framework developed in information design and statistics to enable humans to perceive patterns, relationships, and anomalies in data through visual perception. The encoding is built through sustained practice in visualization design and persists through teaching, conventions, and standards in data representation.

A feature is a human-made property or characteristic extracted or selected from raw data to serve as input for a model or analysis. It is the bridge between raw observations and machine-readable structure, designed to carry predictive signal.

A reliability diagram is a human-made visualization tool used in machine learning and statistics to assess the calibration of probabilistic predictions. It plots predicted probability bins against the observed frequency of the positive class, producing a curve that reveals systematic overconfident or underconfident calibration errors. Built to persist through standard plotting libraries and model evaluation frameworks.

A machine learning paradigm that combines predictions from multiple base models to produce a single improved prediction. Built to persist through established algorithms (bagging, boosting, stacking), academic literature, and widespread deployment in competitive and production settings.

A machine learning ensemble method that trains base learners on bootstrap samples of the training data and aggregates their predictions, built to persist as an algorithmic procedure through software implementations and textbook descriptions.

A supervised learning model that finds the optimal hyperplane separating data points into classes in a high-dimensional feature space, built to persist as a trained mathematical model through software implementations like libsvm and scikit-learn.
A single metric combining precision and recall as their harmonic mean, used to evaluate classification model performance. Human-made statistical construct for summarizing binary-classifier quality.

A hyperparameter tuning methodology that uses Bayesian inference to build a probabilistic surrogate model of the objective function, selecting the next evaluation point by optimizing an acquisition function. Human-made optimization strategy for expensive black-box functions.

A formal branch of mathematical logic that studies collections of objects (sets), their properties, operations (union, intersection, complement), and relationships. Human-invented axiomatic framework (ZFC, NBG, etc.) that serves as a foundation for much of modern mathematics.

A systematic procedure for selecting the optimal hyperparameters — configuration settings that govern the training process of a model — by searching a defined space of possible values. Human-designed optimization practice that persists through documentation, tooling, and scientific literature.

A quantitative measure of uncertainty or information content in a probability distribution — the expected value of the self-information of outcomes.
