Human-designed mathematical concept from information theory, built to persist as a formal quantity used in data compression, statistics, and machine learning.

Probability theory is a human-made formal discipline that models and quantifies uncertainty through axiomatic systems of chance. It provides the mathematical framework for randomness, risk, and inference under ignorance — the map of uncertainty humans built to reason about stochastic phenomena, make predictions, and update beliefs from evidence.

The proportion of actual positives correctly identified by a classifier: recall = TP / (TP + FN). Human-made: a metric invented in information retrieval (1950s) and adopted by machine learning to measure a model's completeness in finding relevant instances.

A numerical measure of impurity or inequality, computed as G = 1 − Σᵢ pᵢ² where pᵢ is the proportion of items belonging to class i. In machine learning it quantifies node impurity in decision-tree splitting (CART); in economics it measures income or wealth dispersion. Human-made: a formula invented by Corrado Gini (1912) and adopted across disciplines as a standard metric.

A cutoff value that transforms a continuous prediction or score into a discrete classification or binary decision — built to persist through standardized protocols in statistics, machine learning, signal detection theory, and clinical diagnostic practice

A human-defined measure of difference between two probability distributions — quantifies how much information is lost when one distribution is used to approximate another. Built to persist as a mathematical construct through formal publication, computational libraries, and use in machine learning, statistics, and information theory.

A human-made visualization technique in statistical decision theory that plots the trade-off between true positive rate and false positive rate across all classification thresholds. Built to persist as a formal analytical instrument used in machine learning, medical diagnostics, and signal detection theory.

A human-made concept in statistical classification that specifies the decision boundary separating positive from negative predictions by a model's output score, built to persist through language and teaching in machine learning and decision theory practice.

A human-made field of study that examines how decisions should be made under uncertainty, combining probability theory, utility theory, and value assessment to prescribe optimal choices. Built to persist through academic discourse, formal models, and applied frameworks in operations research, economics, and artificial intelligence.

A human-made statistical metric that combines precision and recall into a single score using their harmonic mean, used to evaluate the performance of classification models when class balance is uneven. Built to persist through standardization in machine learning evaluation and information retrieval practice.

A human-made statistical function used in machine learning and statistics to measure the performance of a classification model that outputs probabilities. It quantifies the difference between predicted probabilities and actual binary outcomes by computing the negative log-likelihood, penalizing confident wrong predictions exponentially.

A human-made mathematical function from information theory that quantifies the difference between two probability distributions. Built to persist through formal notation and mathematical teaching — it is the expected number of bits needed to identify events from one distribution when using a code optimized for another.
A scalar metric that summarizes the entire ROC curve by computing the area under the curve, measuring a model's discrimination ability across all classification thresholds

Sensitivity is a human-made statistical metric that measures the proportion of actual positive cases correctly identified by a test or classifier. It is a construct of statistical theory and diagnostic evaluation, built to persist through mathematical notation and scientific practice.

Human-made statistical concept for evaluating binary classifiers: the true negative rate, measuring the proportion of actual negatives correctly identified. Built to persist through teaching, medical practice, and statistical methodology.

Human-made statistical concept for evaluating binary classifiers: the proportion of actual negatives incorrectly identified as positives, measured as FP / (FP + TN). Built to persist through teaching, clinical evaluation protocols, and automated model assessment pipelines.

Human-made statistical concept for evaluating binary classifiers: the proportion of actual negatives correctly identified by a test or model, measured as TN/(TN+FP). Built to persist through teaching, medical diagnostics, and machine learning benchmarking as the formal counterpart to recall (sensitivity).

A human-made statistical measure used in binary classification evaluation: the proportion of actual positives that are incorrectly identified as negative, computed as FN/(TP+FN). Built to persist through repeated use in model evaluation, reporting, and comparison of classification systems.

A human-made mathematical function that gives the probability that a real-valued random variable takes a value less than or equal to x — the integral of the probability density function, used to characterize the distribution of random variables

A human-made mathematical construct in classification theory: the hypersurface or threshold in feature space that separates decision regions corresponding to different classes. Built to persist through formal specification in classifiers, enabling deterministic class assignment for any point in the input space.

A human-made mathematical construct in probability theory: a function describing the relative likelihood of a continuous random variable assuming a given value, such that the integral over any interval gives the probability of the variable falling within that interval. Built to persist through teaching, computation, and application in statistics and machine learning.

A human-designed resampling procedure for model evaluation: the dataset is partitioned into k equal-sized folds, and the model is trained k times, each time using k-1 folds for training and the remaining fold as a held-out test set. The procedure persists as a standard practice in machine learning workflows, codified in textbooks and implemented in every major ML framework.

A human-made construct for deliberately fabricated information presented as legitimate journalism — invented to deceive, designed to circulate through media channels for political, financial, or social effect. Persisted by social media platforms, fact-checking institutions, and legal frameworks that define and prosecute it.

a decoy is a fabricated object, signal, or behavior designed to draw attention, effort, or attack away from a genuine target. It exists as both physical artifact (canvas duck, dummy server, placeholder target) and as a conceptual tactic, deployed by deliberate design across hunting, warfare, cybersecurity, wildlife management, and deception operations. It persists through teaching, practice, and material reproduction.

Mutual information is a human-made measure of how much knowing one random variable reduces uncertainty about another. It quantifies the shared information between variables — built to persist through probability theory, statistics, and information theory as a tool for feature selection, dependency detection, and model evaluation.

Decoding is the human-made process of converting encoded information back to its original or interpretable form. It is a constructed procedure — used in communication systems, cryptography, data compression, and symbolic representation — built to reverse the transformations of encoding and persist through standardized algorithms and protocols.

Model comparison is a human-made analytical framework for evaluating and contrasting two or more predictive models against each other using shared criteria such as accuracy, complexity, interpretability, and generalization performance. It is a constructed set of methods and principles — including statistical tests, cross-validation schemes, and information-theoretic scores — built to persist as a systematic way to decide between competing models.

A human-made computational technique in neural networks that allows a model to dynamically weight the importance of different input elements when producing outputs. Built to persist as a mathematical formalism and software implementation across AI research and production systems.

A human-made mathematical technique used in statistics and machine learning to project data from a high-dimensional space into a lower-dimensional one while preserving the structure most relevant to the task. Built to persist as formal algorithms (principal component analysis, t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders) implemented in software libraries and taught across computational disciplines.

A human-made mathematical framework for quantifying how the likelihood of an outcome changes when we know that some other outcome has occurred. Built to persist as a formal rule in probability calculus, enabling inference, prediction, and decision-making under partial information.

A human-made concept in machine learning and statistics describing a situation where one or more classes in a classification dataset are significantly underrepresented relative to others, creating skewed class distributions that affect model training and evaluation.

A human-made mathematical concept measuring the degree of uncertainty, randomness, or information content in a probability distribution or data set. It quantifies the expected value of information contained in a message.

A human-made mathematical theorem relating conditional and marginal probabilities. It provides a principled method for updating beliefs in light of new evidence by combining prior knowledge with observed data through the ratio of likelihood to marginal probability.

A human-made probabilistic classification algorithm based on applying Bayes' theorem with strong independence assumptions between features. Despite its simplistic assumption of feature independence — which is rarely true in practice — it performs competitively on many real-world problems, particularly text classification, spam filtering, and document categorization. The algorithm estimates class probabilities from training frequency counts.

A human-made mathematical function that assigns a single real number to a random variable, representing the long-run average of its outcomes weighted by their probabilities. It is the central moment of a probability distribution and the foundation for measures of dispersion, risk, and rational choice under uncertainty.

A human-made statistical concept representing the initial degree of belief in a hypothesis before observing new evidence. In Bayesian statistics, it is denoted P(H) for hypothesis H and serves as the starting point for Bayes' theorem: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. Priors encode existing knowledge or assumptions and are updated to posterior probabilities upon observing data. Priors can be informative (based on substantive knowledge), non-informative (designed to exert minimal influence), or reference (objective Bayesian choice). The formalization of prior probability is attributed to Thomas Bayes and Pierre-Simon Laplace.

A human-made mathematical framework for quantifying information, uncertainty, and communication, founded by Claude Shannon in 1948. It persists through mathematical formalism, academic teaching, and engineering practice in telecommunications and data compression.

A human-made probabilistic concept representing the updated degree of belief in a hypothesis after observing evidence. It is the output of Bayes' theorem — the conditional probability of a hypothesis given observed data — and persists through mathematical formalism, Bayesian statistical practice, and machine learning inference protocols.

A human-made information-theoretic measure of the information content carried by a single event: the negative logarithm of its probability. Introduced by Shannon, it quantifies how surprising an outcome is — rare events carry high surprisal, common events carry low surprisal. It persists through mathematical formalism, communication theory, and machine learning applications.

A human-made branch of information theory dealing with lossy data compression. It quantifies the minimum achievable data rate at which a source can be reproduced within a specified distortion tolerance. Introduced by Shannon, it extends lossless compression theory to practical scenarios where some information loss is acceptable. It persists through mathematical formalism, signal processing, and compression algorithm design.

A human-made information-theoretic framework for learning compressed representations that retain only the information relevant to a target variable, formalized as an optimization over the trade-off between compression rate and predictive accuracy.

A human-made mathematical function that transforms a neural network's weighted input into an output signal, introducing non-linearity that enables the network to learn complex patterns. Built to persist through software libraries and model architectures.

A symmetric, smoothed measure of the difference between two probability distributions, defined as the weighted average of the KL divergences from each distribution to their midpoint. It is human-made as a formal information-theoretic construct, persisted through its closed-form mathematical definition and used as a distance-like measure in statistics, machine learning, and natural language processing.

A measure of the average uncertainty or information content in a random variable's probability distribution. Quantifies the expected number of bits needed to encode symbols drawn from that distribution. Human-made as a mathematical formalism — defined by Claude Shannon in 1948 as H(X) = -Σ p(x) log₂ p(x) for discrete distributions. Built to persist through information theory, data compression, and statistical inference.

Statistical learning is a framework for building models that generalize from data, combining probability theory with optimization algorithms to infer patterns. It is human-made as a methodological concept bridging statistics and machine learning, built to persist through textbooks, software libraries, and the practice of predictive modeling across scientific and industrial domains.

a human-made mathematical concept from cooperative game theory that assigns a unique distribution of total surplus to each participant based on their marginal contributions across all possible coalitions, built to persist through the Shapley axioms (efficiency, symmetry, dummy, additivity) and computation via coalition enumeration or approximation methods

a human-made metric from probabilistic forecasting that quantifies the gap between predicted confidence and actual accuracy across binned probability estimates, built to persist through computational evaluation and model validation practice

A statistical resampling technique for estimating the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing samples with replacement from an observed dataset. It is a human-invented computational procedure developed by Bradley Efron (1979), built to persist through software implementations and statistical practice.

A human-invented machine learning paradigm where knowledge, representations, or skills acquired in one domain or task are reused and adapted to improve learning in a different but related domain or task. Built to persist through formal algorithms, training protocols, and the ML research literature.

A human-invented system of planning and controlling how time is spent across activities, designed to increase effectiveness and efficiency. Built to persist through techniques, tools, calendars, and organizational practices.

A human-designed practice of structuring choices and choice environments to systematically influence how people decide — including defaults, framing, choice-set curation, and nudge engineering, built to persist through institutional practice and documentation

The systematic adjustment of probabilistic predictions so they match observed frequencies — a practice used in forecasting, machine learning, and decision analysis to make probabilistic judgments reliable

The amount of mental effort, attention, and information-processing capacity required by a task. Human-made as a construct in cognitive psychology and human factors engineering to measure and manage the demands placed on working memory and attentional resources.

A machine learning paradigm where an agent learns optimal behavior through interaction with an environment, receiving reward signals that guide policy updates toward maximizing cumulative future reward.

A scalar feedback value used in reinforcement learning and behavioral engineering to quantify the desirability of an outcome, designed by humans to guide agent or subject behavior toward optimized policy or response selection.

A cognitive bias in which a person's subjective confidence in their judgments, abilities, or predictions systematically exceeds the objective accuracy of those judgments, abilities, or predictions. Human-made as a diagnosed pattern of miscalibration, persisting through social reinforcement of self-assurance and cultural narratives that reward confidence over calibration.

The human-made concept in cognitive psychology describing the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered (the 'anchor') when making decisions. Built to persist through empirical research, teaching in behavioral economics and psychology, and practical application in negotiation and judgment training.

Self-talk is a psychological construct — a human-made technique of deliberate inner dialogue used to regulate emotion, guide behavior, and structure thought. It persists through language, therapeutic practice (especially cognitive behavioral therapy), and everyday application as a tool for self-regulation.

A human-made concept from cognitive behavioral therapy: a systematic pattern of faulty reasoning that produces distorted perceptions of reality. Coined by Aaron Beck in the 1960s, it is a category in clinical psychology for classifying irrational thought patterns such as catastrophizing, black-and-white thinking, and overgeneralization — the map humans use to identify and correct defective reasoning in therapeutic practice.

A deliberate cognitive and communicative technique where one changes the interpretive frame applied to a situation — replacing a default or unhelpful perspective with an alternative one. Used in therapy (CBT), negotiation, leadership, and everyday sense-making. Human-made: it is a learned method, codified in psychology and communication practice, not a natural cognitive process but a structured technique for shifting how meaning is assigned.

A deliberate emotion-regulation technique where one consciously reinterprets the meaning of a situation to alter its emotional impact. Used in cognitive-behavioral therapy and everyday emotional management. Human-made as a named psychological construct with established therapeutic protocols.

A structured psychotherapeutic technique in cognitive-behavioral therapy where maladaptive thought patterns are systematically identified, evaluated against evidence, and replaced with more balanced alternatives. Built by Aaron Beck and colleagues to treat depression and anxiety disorders.

A structured psychotherapeutic approach developed in the 1960s by Aaron Beck, combining cognitive therapy (modifying maladaptive thoughts) with behavioral therapy (modifying maladaptive behaviors) through evidence-based techniques. Built to persist through clinical manuals, training protocols, and academic discipline.

A class of conscious and unconscious processes by which individuals monitor, evaluate, and modify emotional responses — both their own and those of others. Constructed through psychological research, social norms, and therapeutic practice. Persists via teaching, cultural transmission, and clinical application.

A psychological phenomenon where the belief in a treatment's efficacy produces measurable physiological or behavioral effects, even when the treatment is pharmacologically inert. Filed as the named construct used to control expectation in clinical trials — the map of the effect, not any natural biological response.

A human-made mnemonic technique that creates a spatially organized mental environment — rooms, corridors, landmarks — to store and retrieve information through spatial association and visualization. Built to persist through deliberate practice and cultural transmission across learners and traditions.

A cognitive shortcut where individuals rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered (the 'anchor') when making decisions. Subsequent judgments are made by adjusting away from that anchor, and adjustments are typically insufficient. The construct is human-made: it was identified and formalized by Tversky and Kahneman in 1974 as part of research on judgment under uncertainty, and persists through scientific literature, behavioral economics, and applied fields like negotiation and marketing.

A social-psychological concept describing how a false belief or expectation about a situation elicits behaviors that cause the false belief to become true. Coined by Robert K. Merton (1948), it is a human-made theoretical construct used in sociology, psychology, and organizational theory to explain feedback loops in social prediction. Built to persist through academic teaching, discourse, and institutionalized use in social science methodology.

A human-constructed measure of the difference between an expected outcome and the actual outcome — a mathematical quantity used in reinforcement learning, classical conditioning theory, and neuroscience to model how systems update their expectations. The concept was formalized in the Rescorla-Wagner model (1972) and later identified with dopamine neuron activity in the brain. It is a map of a learning signal, not the biological mechanism itself.

A human-constructed concept categorizing the cognitive and affective response to events that violate expectations — the jolt of incongruity that signals the world has diverged from the predicted model, used in psychology, narrative theory, comedy, and epistemic reasoning to mark the gap between expectation and reality.

A human-made system for ordering participants in a line or sequence, used to allocate limited resources or services fairly. It persists through language, teaching, signage, and sustained social practice.

A conscious emotion regulation strategy in which individuals inhibit outward expression of ongoing emotional responses. It is a learned technique, studied in cognitive-behavioral therapy and affective neuroscience, where the internal experience persists but behavioral expression is suppressed.

A system of waste management and hygiene infrastructure designed to protect public health through the collection, transport, and disposal of human waste and wastewater. It is engineered infrastructure maintained by municipalities or public authorities, persisting through civic governance and engineering practice.

A human-made theory in information science that models information-seeking behavior as analogous to animal foraging — people optimize their information-gathering based on the perceived 'value' (information utility) and 'cost' (effort to access) of information sources, developed by Peter Pirolli and Stuart Card in 1999.
Time limits imposed on tasks or projects, used to coordinate collective effort and create urgency. Human-made temporal constraints that convert open-ended work into bounded activity windows.

The Zeigarnik effect is a human-made psychological concept describing the tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones. It is a construct of cognitive psychology, named after Bluma Zeigarnik who first observed and documented this memory bias in the 1920s. The concept maps how task completion status affects memory retention and has been validated through controlled experimental paradigms.

A human-made concept from behavioral psychology (Skinner's operant conditioning) describing a schedule where rewards are delivered after unpredictable intervals or numbers of responses, creating durable behavior patterns resistant to extinction.
The set of psychological processes by which individuals influence which emotions they experience, when they arise, and how they express and manage those emotions.

A human-made cognitive shortcut where the ease of processing information is used as a mental cue for judgment — things that are easier to perceive, remember, or process are judged as more familiar, true, or valuable.

Social proof is a human-made psychological model describing the tendency to look to others' behavior as guidance for one's own actions in uncertain situations. It is a conceptual framework developed in social psychology to explain and predict conformity in ambiguous contexts.

A cognitive bias identified by psychologists Justin Kruger and David Dunning in 1999: individuals with low ability at a task systematically overestimate their competence, because they lack the metacognitive capacity to recognize their own incompetence. A human-made psychological construct that persists through research paradigms, academic teaching, and disciplinary discourse.

A sunset clause is a human-made legal construct: a provision written into a law, regulation, or contract that sets an automatic expiration date or triggers termination upon a specified event, ensuring the provision ceases to operate unless actively renewed or extended by the governing authority.

A human-made linguistic construct: a word that shares the same pronunciation as another word while having a distinct meaning and usually a different origin. Built to persist through language, dictionaries, and linguistic classification.

A human-made psychological construct: a specific cognitive bias where individuals systematically overestimate their abilities, knowledge, or prospects relative to objective reality. Built to persist through language (naming the bias), psychological measurement (benchmarking overestimation), and decision-science practice (correcting for it in judgment).

A human-made aspect of an environment or artifact, intentionally designed or organized, to enable or support a specific cognitive operation — such as a checklist extending working memory, or a color-coded system reducing attentional load. It is made all the way down: the design principles, the artifacts, and the practices of creating them are human outputs that persist through teaching, documentation, and cultural transmission.

A human-made visual marking — parallel lines, spaces, or geometric patterns — designed to encode data for machine reading. Built for persistence through universal standardization in commerce, logistics, and inventory systems, where optical scanners decode the pattern back into structured information.

A human-made two-dimensional matrix barcode — a grid of black and white cells on a square background — designed to encode data for machine reading. Built for persistence through ISO/IEC 16022 standardization in logistics, healthcare, and manufacturing.

Andragogy is the constructed method and theory of adult education — a systematic framework for designing instruction that accounts for adult learners' autonomy, prior experience, and problem-centered orientation. It is human-made, codified by educators since Knowles formalized it in the 1970s, and persists through educational institutions, training programs, and professional development practices.

A machine-readable optical label composed of black modules arranged in a square grid on a white background, encoding data through a standardized pattern of finder symbols, timing patterns, alignment markers, and data cells; designed for high-speed bidirectional scanning with built-in error correction to remain readable when partially damaged.

A design technique where user interface elements visually mimic their real-world counterparts — using textures, shadows, gradients, and forms borrowed from physical objects to make digital interfaces intuitive and familiar. Built to persist through design systems, style guides, and software conventions that propagate across platforms and eras.

A human-made software construct for temporary data holding and transfer: a virtual buffer that holds a copy of data (text, images, files) for subsequent pasting, enabling cut-copy-paste workflows in computing. The concept was coined at Xerox PARC in the 1970s as a desktop metaphor from the physical clipboard, extending the idea of a temporary holding surface into digital interfaces.

A human-made pointed instrument designed for writing, drawing, or interacting with touch-sensitive surfaces. It is a tool that extends the human hand's capacity to apply precise pressure and control to a surface, manufactured from materials such as wood, metal, plastic, or rubber, and persisted through physical fabrication and material culture.
a low-fidelity visual guide depicting the skeletal layout of a digital interface, designed to communicate structural hierarchy and content placement before visual design or interaction is specified

a human-made interface construct that provides reversibility of the most recent action, implemented as a stack of operations that can be walked backward. Built to persist across software applications as a standard interaction primitive since the 1970s.

An initialism is a human-made linguistic construct: a type of abbreviation formed from the initial letters of a multi-word name or phrase, pronounced by articulating each letter individually rather than as a word. It is built to persist through language conventions, teaching, and repeated usage in both writing and speech.
A human-made design artifact: a static visual representation of a product or interface, showing layout, typography, and visual elements without interactivity, used to communicate design intent.

A human-made academic discipline: the systematic study of proper names — their origins, forms, meanings, and usage across languages and cultures. Built to persist through scholarly publication, teaching, and institutional practice.

A human-made software construct — an intermediate layer of code or services positioned between applications and underlying infrastructure, providing common functionality while abstracting implementation details from the applications above it.
A white, smooth writing surface designed for dry-erase markers, where markings are temporary and erasable, used in education and business for visual communication and collaborative display

A separation process in which components of a liquid mixture are separated based on differences in volatility: the mixture is heated to produce vapor richer in the more volatile component, and the vapor is then condensed back into liquid form. Human-made as both a practiced technique (heating, condensing, collecting) and a conceptual framework for purification by differential volatility.

A human-made practice of arranging elements (visual, auditory, textual) into a coherent whole. Built to persist through notation systems, pedagogical traditions, and cross-disciplinary application in art, music, writing, and design.

A human-made design concept: the deliberate use of empty or unmarked area around and between elements in visual composition. Built to persist through design pedagogy, graphic arts practice, and architectural theory — the conscious shaping of absence as a compositional tool.

A metaphor that has undergone conventionalization to the point where competent speakers process it literally rather than figuratively — the figurative origin survives only in etymological trace, not in current cognitive processing. Human-made because it requires the deliberate act of figurative speech followed by the cultural process of linguistic habituation that erases the figurative perception.

The deliberate use of visual elements — color, composition, typography, imagery — to create meaning, evoke response, or persuade an audience. It is human-made through design practice and persists through visual communication conventions, art criticism, and advertising theory.

Refraction is the systematic bending or distortion of meaning, perception, or information as it passes through different interpretive frameworks, cultural contexts, or media. It is human-made through the practices of translation, interpretation, and mediation, and persists through teaching and scholarly discourse in semiotics, communication theory, and cognitive science.

A human-made generative machine learning architecture that learns a probabilistic latent representation of input data through an encoder-decoder structure, enabling generation of new samples by sampling from the learned latent space.

A human-made reasoning method for selecting among competing hypotheses by evaluating which best accounts for the observed evidence, formalized in philosophy of science and widely used in scientific and everyday reasoning

The mental concept or sense that a sign produces in the mind of an interpreter. A human-made semiotic map — not the interpretive act itself but the category of what gets interpreted, as formalized in Peirce's triadic model of sign relations.

The human-made concept of adjusting variables within constraints to maximize or minimize a goal function. It is a formal method — not the natural tendency toward equilibrium — built through mathematics, algorithms, and sustained practice across engineering, economics, and computer science.

The human-made concept of activities, roles, and practices that operate across organizational, disciplinary, or social boundaries. It is an institutional practice — not a natural tendency to cross physical boundaries — sustained through organizational theory, management education, and deliberate institutional design (boundary spanners, liaison roles, interdisciplinary teams). Built to persist via academic study, professional roles, and organizational chart structures.

The human-made concept of deliberately reflecting on experiences, actions, or decisions to extract lessons and improve future performance. It is a construct in educational theory and professional development — not the natural act of reflection, but the structured, systematic practice of deliberate self-examination.
A human-made procedure for selecting a subset from a larger set, designed to represent the whole. Built by statisticians and researchers to make inference from partial data possible.

A human-made learning process that identifies and revises the underlying assumptions, norms, and objectives governing a system's operations. Developed by organizational theorists Chris Argyris and Donald Schön to describe deep, structural learning that transcends surface-level error correction. Built to enable organizations and individuals to adapt their governing frameworks, not just their actions.

A human-made learning process that detects and corrects errors by adjusting actions, strategies, or operations within a fixed set of underlying goals, norms, and assumptions. Developed by organizational theorists Chris Argyris and Donald Schön as the simpler form of organizational learning, contrasted with double-loop-learning. Built for incremental improvement without challenging foundational frameworks.

A human-made cognitive skill that decomposes complex problems into step-by-step procedures, rules, or decision chains. Developed in computer science and now taught as a general problem-solving method across disciplines.

Human-made concept for the investment of attentional and processing resources required to perform a cognitive task. Built to persist through psychological theory, subjective experience of difficulty, and behavioral measurement — it is the map of mental exertion, not the neural events themselves.

Human-made concept for the range or scope of attention that a given framework, discipline, or practice permits. Built to persist through psychological and sociological theory — it is the map of how conceptual systems filter what we can see, not the neural limits of vision itself.

The human-made practice of defining, structuring, and contextualizing a problem before attempting to solve it — choosing the right questions, boundaries, and constraints. Built to persist through teaching, documentation, and methodology across disciplines.

A named observation about distribution patterns — the empirical regularity that roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes. Human-made as a conceptual model used in economics, quality management, and systems analysis to identify disproportionate contributions and prioritize action.

A human-made psychological construct: a predisposition to perceive, interpret, and respond to stimuli in characteristic ways based on prior expectations, mental readiness, and contextual framing. Built to persist through teaching, research, and clinical practice in psychology and cognitive science.

A learning-mechanism is a structured process or system that enables the acquisition, modification, or retention of knowledge or behavior through experience, instruction, or practice. It is human-made in the sense that it is a conceptual framework for organizing how learning occurs — whether instantiated in cognitive science, education theory, or organizational practice.

A cognitive walkthrough is a usability inspection method in which evaluators simulate a first-time user's problem-solving process to identify learnability barriers in an interface. It is human-made: codified by Nielsen, Lewis and colleagues in HCI research, taught in UX curricula, and practiced as a structured evaluation technique. It names the map — the method itself — not the natural act of trying something new.

Self-monitoring is a human-made concept in psychology and organizational behavior: the deliberate tracking and evaluation of one's own thoughts, behaviors, and performance against standards or goals. It is human-made because it requires reflective capacity, intentional design of monitoring practices, and institutionalization through tools like journals, dashboards, or performance reviews.

Categorisation is a human-made cognitive practice: the deliberate act of sorting, grouping, and assigning items into categories based on shared properties or criteria. It is produced and sustained through language, teaching, and institutional classification systems — a map-building activity that orders experience for practical use.

Credibility-assessment is a human-made epistemic practice: the systematic evaluation of a source, claim, or message for reliability, truthfulness, and authority. It is produced through culturally transmitted standards of evidence and sustained through teaching, social enforcement of credibility norms, and institutional verification mechanisms.

A human-made model of how deliberate repetition transforms conscious actions into automatic behaviors, built to persist through repetition schedules, environmental cues, and reward conditioning — frameworks developed by psychologists and behavioral scientists to engineer behavioral change in individuals and populations.

A human-made analytical framework for distinguishing meaningful patterns (signal) from random variation (noise) in observation or measurement. Built to persist through mathematical modeling of decision-making under uncertainty, applied in engineering, medicine, psychology, and all fields requiring threshold-based classification.

A self-regulated learning strategy where learners generate explanations for new information as they encounter it, forcing them to integrate material with prior knowledge, identify gaps, and construct causal narratives. Built to persist through classroom practice, educational research, and curriculum design as a measurable predictor of comprehension and retention.

A learning tool consisting of small cards with information on both sides, used for active recall testing. Built to persist through repeated practice sessions, spaced repetition protocols, and educational production chains.

A collection of human-made techniques, tools, and practices designed to extend or supplement human memory capacity — including writing, external databases, mnemonic systems, and digital storage. Built to persist through cultural transmission, institutional record-keeping, and technological infrastructure that preserves information beyond individual cognitive limits.

A time-management technique where the day is divided into discrete blocks of time, each assigned to a specific task or activity category, with deliberate transitions between blocks. Human-made as a structured productivity method; persists through teaching, scheduling tools, and sustained personal practice.
A time management technique in which a fixed period is allocated for an activity, after which work stops regardless of completion status, forcing prioritization and iterative refinement.

A human-made cognitive tool that structures how a choice is posed — specifying what dimensions matter, what options count, and what the stakes are. The frame is built, not found, and different framings of the same underlying choice can lead to different decisions.

The studied construct of perceiving environmental elements, comprehending their meaning, and projecting their status in near-future scenarios — as formalized in human factors engineering, aviation safety, and emergency response. A framework for measuring and training awareness in complex, dynamic environments.

A structured, human-made process for systematically identifying, analyzing, and documenting potential threats to a system, asset, or organization — as practiced in cybersecurity, risk management, and engineering disciplines. It produces formal threat models that enumerate adversary capabilities, attack vectors, and mitigation strategies.

A human-made accounting construct used in site reliability engineering: the quantified allowance of error or failure a service may accumulate within a defined period before violating its reliability target. Built to persist through SLO definitions, monitoring dashboards, and operational playbooks that translate abstract reliability goals into concrete tolerance thresholds.

A service-level-objective is a human-made target that specifies the desired level of reliability, availability, or performance for a service. It is a formal commitment expressed as a quantified metric over a time window — the contract between service providers and users about what 'good enough' means. Built to persist through documentation, monitoring tooling, and organizational practice.

Observability is a human-made practice in software engineering and operations that defines how to infer a system's internal state from its external outputs — logs, metrics, and traces. It is a conceptual framework built by practitioners to reason about complex systems, not the systems themselves. The concept was coined by Leslie Brown (1976) in control theory and later adapted for software by Michael Nygard (2012).

A human-made discipline in software engineering that applies reliability targets (SLOs), error budgets, and observability practices to ensure system uptime and performance. Built to persist through organizational processes, tooling, and cultural practices.

A human-made incident review practice that investigates failures by focusing on system design and process factors rather than individual blame. Built to persist through structured documentation, organizational learning cycles, and the normalization of psychological safety in technical teams.

A human-made quantified measure that tracks a specific aspect of service performance — latency, throughput, error rate, or availability. Built to persist through monitoring systems, dashboards, and alerting pipelines that collect and display it over time.

A deployment strategy where changes are released to a small subset of users or servers before full rollout, allowing failure detection with minimal blast radius. Human-made: an engineered practice codified in CI/CD tooling and operational procedures to reduce the risk of software releases.

The organizational practice of estimating required production resources—compute, storage, network bandwidth—and provisioning them ahead of demand. Human-made: a management and engineering process documented in capacity-planning frameworks, recurring review cycles, and resource-allocation policies.

A human-made organizational practice for managing and resolving unexpected service disruptions. It involves coordinated actions to identify, contain, remediate, and learn from incidents. Human-made: a structured operational practice codified in IT service management frameworks and organizational procedures.
A software design pattern that prevents cascading failures by stopping calls to a failing service and allowing it time to recover

A human-made engineering technique for containing failures within bounded regions of a system, preventing cascading collapse. Codified in reliability engineering practice, formalized through design patterns (circuit-breaker, bulkhead, timeout), and sustained by tooling (service meshes, sandboxing, resource quotas) and operational discipline (chaos engineering, failure mode analysis).

A human-made system design approach where functionality is intentionally reduced rather than completely lost when components fail, ensuring partial operation under stress. Codified in software engineering and reliability practice as a design strategy for fault resilience.

A human-made engineering concept describing a system's capacity to withstand perturbations and maintain function under stress or adverse conditions. Codified in control theory, structural engineering, and reliability practice as a measurable design property — the map of resilience, not resilience itself.

A human-made engineering practice of intentionally introducing controlled failures into a system to test its resilience, discover weaknesses, and validate that monitoring and recovery mechanisms work correctly under adverse conditions.

A human-made reliability metric that measures the average time elapsed from the detection of a service failure to the restoration of full service operation. It is a quantitative convention used in incident management and SRE practice to benchmark and improve response efficiency.

A human-made contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that defines the expected level of service, including measurable targets, responsibilities, and remedies. It is a formal business construct used in IT service management and cloud computing.

A human-made engineering discipline that applies reliability, availability, and system design principles to build and maintain resilient systems capable of absorbing disruptions, recovering from failures, and adapting to changing conditions.

A structured procedure for transferring operational responsibility, information, and contextual awareness between outgoing and incoming personnel at shift boundaries, built to persist through checklists, logs, and organizational practice

A human-made conceptual framework for quantifying the scope of impact when a system component fails. Built to persist through risk assessment methodologies, architectural design principles, and operational playbooks that contain failure scope.

A human-made design approach that anticipates failure modes and builds systems to handle errors gracefully. Built to persist through engineering standards, design review practices, and safety culture.

A system architecture pattern where a single component's failure causes the entire system to fail. Built to persist through reliability engineering standards, failure mode analysis (FMEA), and system design review practices.

A human-made mechanism that detects an unsafe condition or process deviation and takes automatic action to bring the system to a safe state. Built to persist through safety standards (IEC 61508, IEC 61511, ISO 13849), engineering documentation, regulatory compliance regimes, and physical installation in critical infrastructure.

A human-made analytical construct from safety engineering that identifies hidden flaws, weaknesses, or systemic conditions in an organization or technical system — design deficiencies, management failures, organizational deficiencies — that lie dormant until they combine with active failures to produce an incident. Built to persist through safety investigation frameworks (Reason's Swiss Cheese Model, FMEA, root cause analysis) and safety management standards.

A human-made design concept in reliability and systems engineering that specifies a system should continue operating in a degraded or reduced-capacity mode rather than shutting down entirely when a component fails. The construct distinguishes graceful degradation from catastrophic failure, providing engineers with a design target for availability-critical systems.

A human-made methodology in reliability engineering for systematically identifying, investigating, and characterizing the causes and mechanisms of component or system failures. Built to persist through documented procedures, forensic techniques, and institutional memory in engineering practice.

A human-made systematic strategy for engineering resilience: the deliberate layering of multiple, diverse failure-mitigation controls so that the failure of any single layer does not result in system loss. Built to persist through design standards, engineering practice, and safety regulation.

A human-made safety engineering concept: a failure mode in which two or more redundant components fail simultaneously because they share a root cause — a design flaw, environmental stress, or procedural error that bypasses the independence assumed by redundancy. Built to persist through safety standards, incident investigations, and risk assessments that force systems to account for failures that redundancy alone cannot prevent.

A human-made practice of methodical examination of systems, processes, or components using documented procedures and scheduled routines to identify issues, verify compliance, and assess performance. Built to persist through checklists, protocols, and organizational scheduling — it is the structured application of human attention to maintain quality and catch failures before they propagate.

mean-time-to-repair is a human-made metric used in reliability engineering to quantify the average time required to repair a failed component and restore system functionality. It is calculated from maintenance logs and serves as a key performance indicator for maintenance operations.

mtbf is a human-made reliability metric that quantifies the average elapsed time between successive failures of a repairable system. It is calculated as total operational time divided by the number of failures, and is used by engineers to assess, compare, and predict system durability across mechanical, electronic, and software systems. The metric persists through maintenance logs, reliability databases, and engineering specifications.

safety-survey is a human-made systematic process for collecting and analyzing data about safety conditions, practices, and culture within an organization. It uses structured instruments (checklists, questionnaires, interviews) to measure the state of safety and identify gaps between desired and actual safety performance.

A human-made engineering concept and design criterion that measures how easily a system or component can be repaired, updated, or serviced after deployment. Built to persist through standards, documentation, and maintenance procedures that make reliability actionable.

A human-made signaling device or mechanism designed to draw attention to a specific condition — danger, status change, or required action — through sensory cues such as sound, light, vibration, or text. Built to persist as a purposeful artifact that interrupts normal operation to signal urgency.

A human-made notification system that translates monitored signals into actionable alerts for operators — designed to draw attention to conditions requiring intervention, through structured channels (pagers, dashboards, on-call rotation), prioritized by severity, and governed by runbook procedures.

A human-made organizational practice for coordinating incident response through a structured command hierarchy — assigning specific roles (incident commander, communications lead, technical leads) to manage the flow of information and decisions during a service disruption.

A human-made categorization of failure behaviors — classifying how systems respond to faults by degrading gracefully rather than failing catastrophically. Built to persist through engineering practice, failure analysis, and safety-critical system design.

A category of work defined by Google SRE as manual, repetitive, automated-away, scalable, and disposable tasks that accumulate in service operations and consume engineering capacity without directly improving the service's long-term health. It is human-made through the practice of identifying and classifying operational drudgery so it can be systematically eliminated.

A systematic reliability-engineering method for identifying potential failure modes in a system or process, analyzing their causes and effects, and prioritizing them by severity, occurrence, and detectability to guide corrective action.

A structured human-made practice for examining incidents after resolution to extract lessons, identify systemic causes, and produce action items that prevent recurrence. Conducted by teams as a deliberate organizational process, distinct from casual after-action discussion by its formal scope, documented outputs, and tracked follow-through.

A human-made monitoring practice that probes a system or component with a simple query or request to verify it is operating correctly. Implemented as software probes and codified in operational runbooks, persisted through monitoring tooling and standard operating procedures.

A human-made SRE construct: a numeric or categorical value configured in monitoring systems that, when crossed by a measured signal, triggers an alert. It encodes organizational judgment about acceptable deviation into machine-evaluable form, persisted in configuration management systems and operational runbooks.

A human-made operational practice where a designated person or team remains available outside normal working hours to respond to incidents, alerts, or service disruptions. Its parameters include the rotation schedule, escalation procedures, and response-time expectations. Built to persist through staffing schedules and on-call rotation systems.

A human-made technique of deliberately introducing faults, failures, or anomalies into a system under test, to verify that the system detects, handles, and recovers from errors gracefully rather than catastrophically.

A human-made dedicated physical or virtual space where teams gather during incidents to coordinate response, share information, and make decisions in real time. Built to persist as a structured command environment that centralizes communication during critical events.

A human-made incident coordination point — a dedicated physical location or virtual channel where incident response teams gather to coordinate, track, and communicate during active incidents. Built to persist as a standard incident-management practice through playbooks and SRE protocols.

A human-made organizational practice where incident responses and post-incident reviews focus on systemic fixes and learning rather than individual blame. Built to persist as a cultural norm that encourages transparency, psychological safety, and continuous improvement in technical teams.

A human-made systematic practice of observing, measuring, and tracking system behavior and operational metrics to detect anomalies, track performance, and maintain awareness of system state. Built to persist as a continuous practice embedded in operational culture and technical tooling.

A human-made disciplined practice of intentionally injecting controlled faults, outages, or degradation into production systems to verify that resilience mechanisms (redundancy, circuit-breakers, failover) operate as designed. Built to discover hidden failure modes before users encounter them, and to validate incident response readiness. The practice persists through scheduled exercise cycles, documented playbooks, and the organizational habit of testing assumptions about system behavior under stress.

A human-made tool that randomly injects faults (killing services, introducing latency, or corrupting data) into production systems to test resilience mechanisms. Built to persist as a standardized technique within chaos engineering practice.

A human-made visual modeling technique that represents a system's reliability architecture using interconnected blocks and lines. Each block represents a component and its reliability properties; connections model how component failures propagate through the system. Built to persist as a standardized analytical method in reliability engineering practice.

A human-made reliability metric that quantifies the average elapsed time between successive failures of a repairable system. Calculated as total operational time divided by the number of failures over a defined observation period. Built to persist as a standardized statistical measure in reliability engineering, maintenance planning, and systems safety practice.

A human-made reliability parameter that defines the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time — the point in time to which systems must be restored. Established through business impact analysis as a formal requirement within disaster recovery planning.

A human-made reliability metric that quantifies the average elapsed time from deployment or activation to the first failure of a non-repairable component or system. Calculated as total operational time divided by the number of units that failed. Established through failure data collection and statistical analysis of component lifespans.

A human-made reliability parameter that defines the maximum acceptable duration of service disruption — the target time by which a system must be restored after a failure event. Established through business impact analysis and disaster recovery planning.

A human-made discipline for planning and executing the restoration of critical IT systems, data, and business operations after a major disruption — a construct of procedures, strategies, and protocols designed to minimize downtime and data loss

A human-made representational construct comprising a structured set of symbols, signifiers, and rules for combining them into meaningful expressions. Symbolic systems are designed and maintained by communities to encode, transmit, and manipulate information — encompassing natural languages, formal logics, programming languages, mathematical notations, and conventional sign systems.
A human-made testing technique that deliberately introduces faults or failures into a system to assess its resilience, identify weaknesses, and validate recovery mechanisms.

A human-engineered system that tightly integrates computation, networking, and physical processes through bidirectional feedback loops, where cybernetic algorithms monitor and control physical entities, and physical events in turn affect computations.

A digital twin is a human-made concept in engineering — a virtual replica of a physical entity, process, or system that mirrors its state in real time through continuous data feeds. It persists through software platforms, data pipelines, and industry standards such as ISO 23247.

Human-error is a human-made classification concept in safety engineering, reliability studies, and organizational psychology — a framework for categorizing the ways human actions, omissions, or decisions contribute to system failures. It persists through standardized taxonomies (e.g., Reason's Swiss cheese model, HFACS), training protocols, and incident analysis methodologies built to prevent recurrent failures.

A service mesh is a human-made infrastructure layer in distributed systems — a dedicated network of proxies that manages service-to-service communication without requiring application-level changes. It persists through configuration files and control plane software that orchestrate routing, discovery, and observability across microservices.

A human-made systematic methodology for identifying hazards and operability problems in industrial processes. It uses structured brainstorming sessions with guide words (such as NO, MORE, LESS, REVERSE) applied to process parameters (flow, temperature, pressure, level) to provoke systematic identification of deviations, their causes, consequences, and existing safeguards. Built to persist through documented procedures, trained facilitators, and standardized worksheets.

A human-made practice of monitoring equipment condition through sensor data and analytics to schedule maintenance before failures occur, distinguishing it from reactive maintenance and time-based preventive maintenance by using actual condition data rather than calendar schedules.

A human-made maintenance practice of performing scheduled upkeep at fixed time or usage intervals to prevent equipment failure before it occurs, distinct from condition-based (predictive) and corrective (reactive) approaches.

A human-made reliability metric that quantifies the frequency of failures over a specified period of operation — the count of failures divided by total operating time. Built to persist through mathematical formalization in engineering practice and standardized in reliability standards (IEC 60300, MIL-HDBK-338).

A human-made reliability metric expressing the proportion of time a system is operational and accessible when needed, typically calculated as MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR). Built to persist through mathematical modeling and engineering practice for designing SLAs, capacity planning, and evaluating redundancy strategies in service architectures.

A human-made conceptual and mathematical framework that describes how a system, component, or material deteriorates over time or cumulative usage. Built to persist through modeling standards, simulation software, and reliability engineering practice.

A human-made maintenance discipline that uses real-time measurement of equipment condition parameters — vibration, temperature, oil analysis, acoustic emission — to determine when maintenance is actually needed, replacing fixed-interval schedules with data-driven decisions. Built to persist through standards bodies, sensor firmware, and analytics platforms.

A human-made systematic methodology for determining maintenance requirements based on failure modes, consequences, and criticality analysis. RCM prioritizes maintenance tasks by evaluating what can fail, how it fails, and the impact of each failure — establishing prevention strategies proportional to risk. Developed by Nowlan and Heap for the airline industry, it is a structured practice for optimizing maintenance investment in engineered systems.

A specialized bar-and-line chart that ranks categories by frequency or impact in descending order, with a cumulative percentage line showing the combined contribution of each category. Built on the Pareto principle (the 80/20 rule) to highlight the vital few causes that generate the majority of effects. Persists through quality management practice, statistical software tooling, and the standardized visual convention of ordered bars overlaid with a running-total curve.

A systematic practice of monitoring equipment parameters (vibration, temperature, pressure, acoustic emissions) during operation to detect early signs of degradation and predict failures before they occur. Human-made as a structured engineering discipline codified by ISO standards and industry bodies.

Statistical process control is a human-made quality management method that uses statistical techniques to monitor and control a process, ensuring it operates at its full potential. It was developed in the 1920s by Walter A. Shewhart at Bell Labs and later refined by W. Edwards Deming. The method persists through standardized procedures, control charts, and institutional knowledge in manufacturing and service industries.

A quality control technique in which a subset of items is inspected to make a decision about accepting or rejecting an entire production lot, based on pre-specified acceptance criteria and statistically designed sampling plans.

A line graph of measured values plotted in chronological order, used to detect trends, shifts, and patterns in a process over time. Human-made as a disciplined practice of data recording and visualisation for process monitoring, persistence through standardised plotting conventions and software implementations.

A statistical measure of how well a manufacturing or business process can produce output within prescribed specification limits, quantified using metrics like Cp and Cpk to compare process variation against allowable tolerance bands.

A statistical process control chart that plots subgroup means over time to detect shifts in the process average. Human-made as a structured visual tool for manufacturing quality monitoring, built to persist through standardized charts and software implementations.

A statistical measure (such as Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk) that quantifies how well a process meets specification limits. Human-made as a quantitative metric for assessing process performance relative to tolerances.

A systematic human-made methodology for planning, conducting, and analyzing controlled tests to study how multiple input factors influence output responses — structured through formal design types (factorial, fractional factorial, response surface, Taguchi) to extract causal relationships with minimum experimental effort.

A structured, proactive technique for identifying potential failures in a product design, analyzing their effects, and prioritizing corrective actions before manufacturing begins — built to persist through engineering documentation, checklists, and lessons-learned databases

A visual representation of a process showing its steps, decision points, and flow — a human-made documentation tool built to persist organizational knowledge and enable process analysis, optimization, and communication.

A human-made representation of events arranged along a chronological axis, used to visualize temporal relationships, sequences, and durations. Persisted through drawings, diagrams, software, and printed media.

A human-made visual representation showing the connections and relationships between discrete entities (nodes) through linking lines (edges), used in project management, systems engineering, sociology, and computer science to model structure, flow, and topology. Persisted through software tools, printed diagrams, and digital collaboration platforms.

An empirical cumulative distribution function plot is a human-made graphical method that plots the proportion of data points less than or equal to each value as a right-continuous step function, constructed by sorting observations and computing cumulative proportions — a deterministic method for visualizing the full shape of an empirical distribution without assuming any parametric form, persisting through statistical software implementations and standard exploratory data analysis practice.

A human-made analytical construct: a class of plots designed to evaluate the adequacy of a statistical model by revealing patterned departures from assumption — residual plots, Q-Q plots, calibration curves, leverage plots. Invented by statisticians as a disciplined practice for model checking; persists through teaching, software defaults, and sustained scientific practice.

A human-made statistical visualization: a plot that displays the leverage of each data point in a regression analysis, showing how far each predictor value lies from the center of the predictor space. Built to persist through statistical software packages and data analysis workflows.

A human-made visualization technique in machine learning interpretability: a plot that displays SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values to show how each feature contributes to a model's prediction for individual instances. Created by Scott Lundberg and Haruki Lee as part of the SHAP framework, these plots map feature importance and direction of influence in model outputs.

A human-made diagnostic visualization that shows how a model's output or parameters change as one or more input variables are varied while others are held constant. Built to persist as a tool for diagnosing model behavior, identifying nonlinear relationships, and communicating how sensitive predictions are to individual inputs.

A human-made statistical measure used in regression analysis to quantify the influence of each observation on the fitted values. Built to persist as a scalar diagnostic computed from regression coefficients and residuals, enabling comparison across observations.

A square matrix used in linear regression that maps observed response values to fitted values (ŷ = Hŷ). It is a human-made mathematical construct, central to regression diagnostics because its diagonal elements (the leverages) quantify how much each observation influences its own fitted value.

A diagnostic visualization in regression analysis that plots the square root of absolute standardized residuals against fitted values, designed to detect heteroscedasticity — non-constant variance of errors across the range of predictions. It is a human-made mathematical construct, persisted through graphical formalism and statistical software implementations.
A subset of data reserved for training machine learning models, consisting of input-output pairs used to adjust model parameters through iterative optimization during the learning process

A human-made collection of data instances organized for storage, analysis, or training. Created, curated, and maintained by humans, it persists as structured data (tables, arrays, records) and serves as the foundational input for machine learning, statistics, and data science.

A human-made directed graph that represents causal relationships between variables: nodes stand for variables and directed edges encode direct causal influences. Built to persist as a formal model used in causal inference, epidemiology, and machine learning for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals.

A human-made regression diagnostic visualization that shows the relationship between a single predictor and the response, after accounting for all other predictors in the model — also called a partial regression plot. Built to persist as a chart type in statistical practice and textbooks.

A human-made statistical measure that quantifies how much the variance of a regression coefficient is inflated by multicollinearity among predictors. Computed as 1/(1-R²) where R² is the R-squared from regressing one predictor on all others.

A propensity score is a human-made statistical construct representing the probability of a unit receiving a treatment or exposure, conditional on a set of observed covariates. It is a tool for reducing confounding bias in observational studies, enabling近似-randomization through matching, stratification, weighting, or adjustment.

A partial residual plot is a human-made statistical visualization used in regression analysis to examine the relationship between a response variable and a single predictor, while accounting for the effects of other predictors in the model. It is constructed by plotting partial residuals (the sum of the raw residuals and the contribution of a single predictor) against that predictor's values, enabling visual diagnosis of nonlinearity, omitted-variable bias, and functional form misspecification. Built to persist as a standard diagnostic tool in statistical practice.

A partial regression plot is a human-made statistical visualization tool used in regression analysis. It displays the relationship between a response variable and a single predictor variable after accounting for the effects of all other predictors in the model, allowing visual assessment of linearity, outliers, and the marginal contribution of each predictor.

Busywork is a human-made category of activity designed to appear productive while achieving little or no real value. It is a social and organizational construct — a practice maintained in workplaces, bureaucracies, and institutions to create the appearance of effort, compliance, or progress without substantive output. The concept persists through language (the word itself signals critique), through organizational behavior patterns, and through the shared recognition that some work exists to look like work rather than to accomplish it.

A studentized residual is a human-made statistical diagnostic: a residual value standardized by an estimate of its standard deviation, enabling comparison across observations and identification of outliers in regression models.

Bootstrapping is a human-made statistical method that estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing random samples with replacement from the observed data. It is a computational technique that uses resampling to quantify uncertainty without parametric assumptions.

A tolerance interval is a human-made statistical construct that quantifies uncertainty in a population: it specifies a range that, with a stated confidence level, contains at least a specified proportion of the population distribution. Unlike confidence intervals (which estimate population parameters) or prediction intervals (which bound single future observations), tolerance intervals jointly specify both coverage proportion and confidence — making them a distinct construct for population-level uncertainty statements. It persists through mathematical formulation and statistical practice.

A human-made statistical construct that standardizes residuals by dividing each residual by an estimate of its standard deviation, enabling comparison across observations and identification of outliers in regression models. It is a map of a data-transformation procedure, not a natural phenomenon.

A human-made statistical measure in regression diagnostics that quantifies the change in each regression coefficient when a single observation is deleted. For observation i and coefficient j, dfbeta_j(i) = (beta_j - beta_j(i)) / SE(beta_j(i)), enabling detection of observations that disproportionately influence individual predictors.
A human-made regression diagnostic measure that quantifies the standardized change in a model's fitted values when a single observation is deleted from the fitting data.

A regression diagnostic visualization that displays component leverage values for each observation, showing how much each predictor contributes to a point's overall leverage. It is a human-made analytical tool used by statisticians to identify influential observations in multivariate regression.

A human-made methodological framework in statistics consisting of tools and techniques designed to assess the validity of regression model assumptions, identify influential observations, and detect model misspecification. It persists as a standardized practice taught in statistical methodology and implemented in statistical software packages.

A human-made statistical measure in regression analysis that quantifies the influence of each observation on the fitted regression coefficients — how much the model changes if a single data point is removed

A human-made statistical measure in regression analysis where raw residuals are divided by an estimate of their standard deviation, producing scale-invariant quantities that enable comparison across observations with differing leverage

A concept in statistical practice identifying data points whose influence on model estimation disproportionately exceeds their proportion in the dataset — quantified through measures such as Cook's distance, DFBETAS, dfits, and leverage.

A quantitative statistic computed from a fitted statistical model to assess its fit, identify problematic observations, or validate assumptions — including Cook's distance, dfits, leverage, and residual-based diagnostics.

A human-made diagnostic visualization constructed by plotting observed quantiles of residuals against theoretical quantiles of a normal distribution, built to persist as a standard diagnostic tool in statistical software for checking the normality assumption in regression models.

A regression diagnostic measure that quantifies the change in each fitted regression coefficient when a single observation is deleted from the model. Built to persist through statistical computing practice and diagnostic reporting conventions.

A leverage residual is a human-made diagnostic construct in regression analysis. It is the product of a raw residual and the square root of the corresponding leverage value (h_ii) from the hat matrix, used to identify observations that exert disproportionate influence on regression coefficient estimates. It persists as a computed quantity within statistical software packages and published regression output tables.

A human-made statistical methodology for modeling the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. Built through mathematical formalization, iterative estimation procedures, and sustained practice in data science, engineering, and the empirical sciences. Persists through computational tools, peer-reviewed methodology, and formal teaching in quantitative disciplines.

A human-made visualization in regression analysis that displays the relationship between a single predictor and the response variable by plotting the predictor values against the sum of the fitted values and the residuals — designed to help detect non-linear relationships and assess the functional form of predictors in a regression model.

model capacity is a human-made concept in machine learning and statistics describing the ability of a model class to approximate complex functions — defined by its structural parameters, architecture, and representation power, and persisting through formal analysis in learning theory and practical calibration during training

Human-made classification systems that organize concepts, objects, or phenomena into hierarchical categories based on shared characteristics. Taxonomies are built through deliberate acts of categorization and are used across domains — from biology and library science to ontology engineering — to enable navigation, retrieval, and structured reasoning about the things they classify.
Human-made set of statistical methods designed to assess whether individual observations in a dataset exert disproportionate influence on the estimated parameters or predictions of a fitted model.

Human-made statistical measure used in regression diagnostics to assess how much deleting a single observation changes the estimated covariance matrix of the regression coefficients — a quantified summary of that observation's influence on parameter uncertainty.
