Human-made methodology encompassing the statistical methods and visualizations used to evaluate regression model assumptions, detect influential observations, and assess model fit. It includes diagnostic measures (leverage, Cook's distance, covariance ratio) and diagnostic plots (residual plots, normal probability plots) that collectively validate regression analysis.

Human-made criterion framework for assessing and categorizing language proficiency levels — the constructed scale and standards (CEFR, TOEFL bands, ACTFL ratings) that map onto the natural ability, not the ability itself

A leave-one-out residual in regression analysis — the residual computed by fitting the model to all observations except one and then calculating the difference between the omitted observation's actual value and the prediction made by that reduced model.

A statistical hypothesis test for first-order autocorrelation in the residuals of a regression model, computed as the ratio of the sum of squared consecutive residual differences to the sum of squared residuals. Built to persist as a routine diagnostic step in regression assumption checking.

A human-made statistical test for detecting heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance of errors) in regression models. It works by regressing squared residuals on explanatory variables and testing whether they explain significant variation — built to persist through statistical practice and software implementation.

DFFIT is a regression diagnostic measure that quantifies the change in the fitted value for observation i when that observation is removed from the regression model. It compares the predicted value using all data against the predicted value computed with leave-one-out fitting, standardized by an estimate of its standard error, making it scale-independent and interpretable across different regression models.

Conformity is a human-made social-psychological concept describing the phenomenon where individuals adjust their behavior, beliefs, or expressions to align with group norms or expectations. It is a studied construct in psychology and sociology, with operational definitions (Asch paradigm, normative/social influence scales) that persist through experimental protocols, teaching, and cultural analysis.

Robust statistics is a human-made branch of statistical methodology concerned with developing procedures whose performance is not unduly degraded by violations of model assumptions, such as the presence of outliers, heavy-tailed error distributions, or data contamination. It was formalized in the 1960s–1970s by Tukey, Hampel, and others as a systematic response to the fragility of classical estimators under realistic data conditions. The concept persists through statistical practice, textbooks, and software implementations.

A human-made methodological category of statistical practices for evaluating whether a fitted statistical model satisfies its assumptions and adequately captures the data-generating process. It persists through standardized diagnostic tests, graphical methods, and formal procedures taught in statistical practice. Model diagnostics include residual analysis, influence examination, specification testing, and goodness-of-fit assessment.

A human-made practice and methodology of evaluating language proficiency through tests, rubrics, and standardized frameworks. It persists through testing institutions, certification bodies, and pedagogical practice — from TOEFL and IELTS to classroom rubrics and proficiency interviews.

A human-made practice of systematically identifying data points that deviate markedly from a dataset's dominant pattern. It persists through statistical software implementations, analytical workflows, and domain-specific practices in quality control, fraud detection, and scientific discovery.

A human-made framework for evaluating whether a statistical or computational model adequately represents the phenomenon it is designed to capture, built through iterative comparison against empirical evidence and peer-reviewed methodology

A statistical concept that measures how well a model's predictions or theoretical distributions match observed data. It provides quantitative indices (chi-squared, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, AIC, R-squared) for evaluating model adequacy — a human-made evaluation metric built to persist through statistical practice.

A human-made statistical concept describing the condition in multiple regression where predictor variables are substantially correlated, preventing precise estimation of individual predictor effects. Built to persist through statistical practice and model diagnostics.

A concept from statistical learning theory that characterizes the gap between a model's performance on its training data and its performance on unseen data drawn from the same distribution. It is a human-made analytical construct — the difference between empirical risk (measured on training data) and expected risk (true performance) — built to persist as the foundational metric for diagnosing overfitting, guiding model selection, and setting expectations about what any trained model can achieve in production.

A technique in machine learning where a model trained on a broad dataset is further trained on a narrower, task-specific dataset to adapt its learned representations for a targeted application domain. Human-made, documented in ML literature, persisted through versioned model checkpoints and model hubs.

A human-made machine learning approach where a system is designed to learn how to learn — the map of techniques that use experience across multiple tasks or training episodes to improve the efficiency or effectiveness of subsequent learning, rather than learning a single fixed mapping from inputs to outputs.

A human-made machine learning architecture that combines a pretrained language model with an external knowledge retrieval system: the model queries a knowledge store to gather relevant context, then generates responses conditioned on both its internal parameters and the retrieved passages. Built to extend model knowledge beyond training data and to ground outputs in specific sources.

A human-made machine learning training technique in which a compact 'student' model learns to replicate the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model by minimizing the divergence between their output distributions. Created by Hinton et al. (2015) and documented across papers, codebases, and industry practice — it persists as a repeatable method for compressing model knowledge into smaller, faster deployments.

A human-made machine learning concept: a pre-trained model whose outputs (predictions, embeddings, or representations) serve as training targets for a smaller student model. It is an institutionalized practice in knowledge distillation, persisted through code implementations and training protocols.

A human-made machine learning practice: the systematic reduction of a trained model's size, parameter count, or computational requirements while preserving predictive performance. Institutionalized through techniques like pruning, quantization, and distillation, it persists as a research field and engineering discipline.

A human-made machine learning concept: a model trained to mimic the outputs or internal representations of a larger teacher model, typically for compression or efficiency purposes. Institutionalized in knowledge distillation research and practice.

A human-made machine learning concept: an approach to learning data representations automatically from raw inputs, rather than hand-crafting features. Institutionalized through decades of ML research as a core paradigm for enabling downstream tasks like classification, detection, and generation by learning useful intermediate abstractions.

Training data is the curated collection of examples humans create, label, and organize to teach machine learning models. It is human-made through selection, annotation, and structuring of raw observations, and persists as reusable datasets that encode the patterns models must learn.

A human-made practice: the systematic assessment of machine learning model performance using defined metrics, held-out datasets, and benchmark protocols. Built to persist through established methodologies, published benchmarks, and shared evaluation frameworks that enable comparison across models and iterations.

Early stopping is a human-made regularization technique in iterative machine learning: the practice of halting model training when a held-out validation metric ceases to improve, thereby preventing overfitting to training data while preserving generalization capacity.

Human-made mathematical construct in control theory and signal processing: the representation of the input-output relationship of a linear time-invariant system as a function of a complex variable (Laplace or Z domain). It is the ratio of output transform to input transform with zero initial conditions — a map that engineers use to analyze system behavior, design controllers, and predict frequency response.

Human-made optimization technique in machine learning training: adjusting the learning rate — the step-size parameter of the optimizer — according to a predefined schedule over training steps or epochs, to balance rapid convergence with fine-grained refinement.
Human-made regularization technique in neural network training: randomly deactivating a fraction of neurons during each training step to prevent co-adaptation and reduce overfitting.

Human-made search methodology for finding the best configuration of hyperparameters — learning rates, layer counts, regularization strengths — in machine learning model training, using algorithms like grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimization.

Human-made neural network training technique: normalizing the activations of each layer across the mini-batch to produce zero-mean unit-variance outputs, reducing internal covariate shift and enabling higher learning rates.

Weight decay is a human-made regularization technique used in training neural networks and other statistical models. It adds a penalty term proportional to the squared L2 norm of the model's weights to the loss function, constraining model capacity and preventing overfitting by discouraging large weight values. It persists as a standard option in optimization frameworks (e.g., SGD with weight_decay) and is a fundamental component of modern training pipelines.

Gradient clipping is a human-made regularization technique used in training neural networks. It limits the magnitude of gradients during backpropagation to prevent exploding gradients, ensuring stable learning dynamics.

Backpropagation is a human-made algorithm for computing gradients in computational graphs and neural networks. It propagates error signals backward through layers using the chain rule of calculus, enabling gradient-based optimization of parameters. It persists as a systematic procedure implemented in all major training frameworks.

The chain rule is a human-made mathematical rule for computing derivatives of composite functions. It states that the derivative of f(g(x)) equals f'(g(x)) × g'(x). It persists as a formal theorem in calculus and a fundamental computational procedure in automatic differentiation.

A human-made computational procedure that systematically adjusts parameters to minimize or maximize an objective function. It persists as formal algorithms in mathematics, machine learning, and operations research — encoded in textbooks, software libraries, and training pipelines.

A human-made design specifying the layer structure, connectivity patterns, and parameter organization of a neural network. It persists as formal specifications encoded in model definitions, architecture papers, and deep learning frameworks that define how information flows through interconnected processing units.

A human-made algorithm that determines how model parameters are updated in response to computed gradients during training. It persists as formal algorithms implemented in computational libraries and frameworks.

A training loop is a human-made procedural construct in machine learning: an iterative cycle that repeatedly feeds data through a model, computes error, computes gradients, and updates parameters — designed to persist as a structured algorithm executed by training frameworks and scripts.

A human-made hyperparameter in machine learning: a scalar value that controls the magnitude of parameter updates during optimization. It is a tunable knob set by practitioners to balance convergence speed against training stability, and persists as a standard concept taught in every ML curriculum and implemented in every training framework.

A learning rate schedule is a human-designed protocol for adjusting the learning rate during training — specifying when and how to reduce, increase, or otherwise modulate the step size parameter. It is built to persist across training runs as a reusable configuration pattern that improves convergence by matching the optimization dynamics to the loss landscape's geometry.

Optics is the human-built field of study investigating the behavior and properties of light, including its interactions with matter and the construction of instruments that use or detect it. It is a branch of physics formalized through mathematical models, experimental methods, and pedagogical traditions across centuries.

Batch size is the human-made parameter in machine learning training that specifies how many training samples are processed through a neural network before the model's internal parameters (weights) are updated. It is a design choice made by practitioners to balance computational efficiency, convergence speed, and generalization quality.

Iteration is the human-made practice of repeating a process or sequence of operations to progressively approach a desired result. It is a procedural construct used in computing, mathematics, manufacturing, and organizational workflows — designed to persist as a repeatable cycle through documentation, algorithms, and standard operating procedures.

The human-made optimization technique of dividing a training dataset into small subsets (mini-batches) and computing a stochastic gradient estimate from each subset to update model parameters iteratively, balancing the computational efficiency of batch methods with the convergence properties of stochastic methods.

One complete pass of a machine learning model through the entire training dataset during training. It is a training hyperparameter that controls how many full dataset cycles the optimization procedure performs.
A human-made household appliance that automates the cleaning of textiles using water, detergent, and mechanical agitation. Built to persist as a durable good for decades of repeated cycles.

A human-made signal processing technique that combines data from multiple heterogeneous sensors to produce a more accurate and reliable estimate than any single sensor could provide. Built to persist as software and firmware implementations in navigation, robotics, and industrial monitoring systems.

A human-made transducer device that converts physical, chemical, or biological parameters into measurable electrical signals for monitoring, control, or analysis. Built to persist as a core component across instrumentation, automation, and computing systems.

A touchscreen is a human-made display surface embedded with a touch-sensing panel that detects finger or stylus input, converting physical contact into electrical signals the device interprets as commands. Built to persist as a hardware interface standard.

A human-made technology that uses touch, force, or vibration to convey information through the sense of touch. Built by engineers and designers for human-machine interfaces, it persists through manufactured actuators (motors, piezoelectric elements) and embedded control firmware.

A human-made mathematical concept: the vector of partial derivatives of a multivariable function, pointing in the direction of steepest ascent. Built to persist through formal notation, teaching in calculus/optimization, and computation in numerical methods.

A human-made pointing tool designed to interact with capacitive touchscreens by mimicking the electrical properties of a human fingertip. Built to persist through manufacturing specifications, ergonomic design standards, and consumer product ecosystems.

A human-made computational technique for identifying intentional human movements from sensor data (camera images, depth sensors, inertial measurements). Built to persist through standardized algorithms, training datasets, and implementation protocols across consumer devices and industrial systems.

A condition in machine learning where a model lacks sufficient capacity to capture the underlying pattern in training data, producing high error on both training and test sets. Built to persist through diagnostic plots (learning curves) and hyperparameter tuning protocols.

A human-made construct in human-computer interaction: any system-generated signal — visual, auditory, or tactile — designed to communicate the state, result, or progress of a user's action back to the operator. Built to persist through UI/UX conventions, system APIs, and interaction design frameworks.

A design element whose appearance references an analog predecessor, even when the functional relationship to that predecessor has been lost in the new medium. Examples: the trash can icon on desktops, the green felt of a digital casino table, the leather-stitched look of a note-taking app. The construct persists through design practice and user-experience convention.

A human-made construct in human-computer interaction and design: the degree to which a product, system, or service enables specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. Usability is not a property of the artifact alone but of the interaction between artifact, user, and task — it is measured and improved through iterative testing, heuristic evaluation, and user-centered design practices.

A human-made construct in psychology and neuroscience: the internal sense of satisfaction or pleasure that reinforces behavior independently of any external reward, arising when an activity itself engages the brain's reward systems without need for extrinsic incentives.

A human-made abstraction for representing real-world phenomena using mathematical structures and probability theory. It is built to persist through formal notation, peer review, and systematic teaching in disciplines that infer patterns from data.

A human-made mathematical discipline that studies graphs — structures made of vertices connected by edges — and their properties. Built to persist through axiomatic formalism, algorithmic computation, and widespread application across computer science, network science, and operations research.
A human-made sequence of processing stages where output from one stage feeds directly into the next, designed to persist as a repeatable workflow across data, manufacturing, or CI/CD contexts.
A human-made graphical method for comparing the distribution of observed data against a theoretical probability distribution, using standardized axes to visually assess distributional fit.

A human-made graphical method for comparing two empirical probability distributions by plotting their quantiles against each other, enabling visual assessment of whether the distributions share a common location, scale, and shape. Persisted through scientific visualization and statistical practice.

A human-made two-dimensional graphical technique that represents three or more quantitative variables on axes radiating from a common origin, with values plotted along each axis and connected to form a polygon, enabling visual comparison of profiles across multiple dimensions.

A method of statistical inference using Bayes' theorem to update the probability of a hypothesis as new evidence becomes available. Human-made through probability theory, persists through computation, scientific practice, and decision theory.

A statistical measure expressing the difference between two group means in units of standard deviation. Human-made through meta-analytic practice, persists through statistical reporting standards and computational methods (Cohen's d, Hedges' g) that standardize effect reporting across studies.

A range of values, computed from sample data, that is predicted to contain a future individual observation with a specified probability. Human-made through statistical inference practice, persists through predictive modeling, quality control, and forecasting standards.

The process of detecting, correcting, or removing corrupt, inaccurate, incomplete, or irrelevant records from a dataset to improve data quality. Human-made through data science and statistical practice, persists through procedural documentation, software tools, and organizational workflow.

A statistical concept specifying the number of independent values in a calculation that are free to vary. It is human-made as a formal parameter in inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing — built to persist through mathematical practice, teaching, and the operation of statistical methods.

A human-made statistical concept describing the bias that arises in regression estimation when a relevant predictor variable is excluded from the model. Built as an analytical framework in econometrics and statistics for diagnosing model misspecification, it persists through teaching traditions, diagnostic checklists, and the formal theory of estimation.

A human-made statistical procedure for evaluating evidence about a population parameter using sample data. Built as a formal decision framework with null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, and significance thresholds. Persists through scientific method, statistical education, and regulatory practice.

A human-made statistical procedure for evaluating evidence about a population parameter or model assumption, using sample data to produce a decision rule. Built with formal hypotheses, test statistics, sampling distributions, and significance thresholds. Persists through textbooks, software implementations, and academic practice.

A statistical concept humans made to measure the correlation of a signal with its own lagged values. It quantifies how data points at one time relate to data points at previous times, enabling detection of patterns like seasonality and trend in time-series data.

A human-made concept in metrology and statistics that quantifies the difference between a measured value and the true value of a quantity. It is the structured framework humans built to characterize, classify, and manage uncertainty in measurement — from systematic and random components to their propagation through calculations. The concept persists through statistical theory, engineering practice, and the calibration infrastructure of science.

A human-made statistical methodology: a computational resampling procedure that estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing samples with replacement from the observed data. Built to persist through algorithmic implementation in statistical software.

A statistical construct that maps each possible value of a sample statistic to its probability under repeated sampling from a population. It is human-made — a formal abstraction built to organize inference about estimators, and it persists through mathematical teaching, computational practice, and the architecture of every statistical procedure.

few-shot-learning is a human-made machine learning approach where a model learns to perform a task from only a small number of training examples, typically by leveraging prior knowledge from related tasks or meta-learning objectives

A training paradigm in machine learning where supervision signals are derived from the input data itself rather than from external human annotation — built to enable models to learn representations at scale from raw, unlabelled corpora.

The classification of computational problems according to the resource demands — time, space, and communication — required to solve them. Built to persist through formal mathematical notation, algorithmic analysis practices, and the theoretical framework that guides what is practically solvable.

A human-made threshold in statistical hypothesis testing — the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true null hypothesis), typically set at 0.05 or 0.01. Built to persist through standardized α notation and decision protocols that determine whether observed evidence constitutes sufficient grounds to reject the null hypothesis.

a human-made mathematical concept that models an objective function as a terrain where coordinates represent parameters and altitude represents loss, built to persist through visualization tools and optimization algorithms

a human-made training strategy in machine learning where training examples are deliberately ordered — typically from simple to complex — so that the learner builds foundational skills before encountering harder cases, built to persist through pedagogical practice in model training pipelines
a human-made mathematical construct that organizes abstract representations of data into a structured coordinate system, built to persist through computational frameworks and measurement tools

A mathematical construct that maps every possible configuration of parameters in a system to a scalar value representing how well that configuration satisfies a specified goal. Built by mathematicians and engineers to formalize the notion of 'goodness' or 'quality' in optimization, design, and learning problems. The mapping is human-authored, persists through notation and software implementations, and is the central artifact that optimization procedures act upon.

A human-authored optimization algorithm that approximates the true gradient of an objective function by computing it on small random subsets (mini-batches) of data, enabling scalable learning in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Built by statistical learning theorists and implemented in optimization libraries.

Information retrieval is a human-made discipline for organizing, storing, and retrieving information from collections. It is defined by: (1) a document collection (text, images, or structured data), (2) a query or information need expressed by a user, (3) an indexing mechanism that maps content to searchable representations, and (4) a ranking or retrieval algorithm that returns relevant results. It persists through search engine architectures, index structures (inverted indices, BM25, vector embeddings), and query processing pipelines, with the goal of maximizing relevance and minimizing latency.

A human-made model trained to predict a scalar reward signal for guiding the fine-tuning of language models via reinforcement learning. It maps text completions to preference scores derived from human comparative judgments, serving as the optimization target in RLHF pipelines. Built to persist through training data, architecture specifications, and deployment as the scoring function in preference-based model alignment.

A human-made class of reinforcement learning methods that optimize a parameterized policy by computing gradients of expected cumulative reward with respect to policy parameters, enabling agents to learn behavior through trial-and-error interaction with an environment.

The human-made discipline of systematic study of natural phenomena — matter, energy, and their interactions. Built as a formal framework of models, experiments, and mathematical description that persists through institutions, publications, and teaching.

A human-constructed metric in cognitive psychology that quantifies the maximum amount of information an individual can hold and manipulate simultaneously in working memory, operationalized through standardized tasks (span tests, n-back, change detection) and treated as a stable trait variable in individual differences research.

A cognitive construct describing the process by which repeated performance of a skill leads to improved speed and accuracy with progressively reduced conscious effort and working-memory load. The phenomenon marks the transition from effortful, controlled processing to rapid, automatic execution — a key mechanism in skill acquisition and expertise development. Persists through language, cognitive-psychology research, and pedagogical theory.
A branch of machine learning concerned with discovering hidden structure in unlabeled data, where algorithms infer patterns without external feedback or labeled training signals.
A human-constructed model designed to forecast future outcomes from observed data, built through training on historical patterns and maintained through periodic re-estimation.

A human-constructed model describing the transformation of labile memories into stable long-term representations. The model partitions consolidation into two tiers — synaptic consolidation (local, minutes to hours, mediated by protein synthesis at synapses) and systems consolidation (distributed, hours to years, involving cortical reorganization). The concept persists through empirical paradigms (retrograde amnesia gradients, sleep-dependent reactivation), computational models of synaptic plasticity, and clinical frameworks for memory disorders.

A human-constructed approach to machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with multiple hierarchical layers to learn increasingly abstract representations from data. Built through engineered architectures (CNNs, RNNs, transformers) and optimized via backpropagation across layered weight matrices.

Working memory training is a class of human-designed cognitive interventions that use structured, adaptive exercises to improve an individual's working memory capacity. It is a therapeutic and educational construct — a methodology built through cognitive science research, operationalized as specific protocols (e.g. n-back tasks, span training) that adapt difficulty based on performance to maintain optimal challenge.

A statistical measure is a human-constructed quantitative metric used in statistics to summarize, describe, or evaluate properties of data distributions. It is built to persist as a standardized tool for statistical inference and description.

Episodic memory is a human-constructed category in cognitive psychology and neuroscience, denoting the system for recalling specific personal experiences embedded with temporal and spatial context — what happened, where, and when. Proposed by Endel Tulving as distinct from semantic memory, it is built to persist as a theoretical construct in memory research, consciousness studies, and clinical neuropsychology.

A human-constructed concept in measurement and systems theory, denoting the maximum amount that a system, container, or entity can hold, produce, or withstand. It is built to persist as a standardized quantitative concept across scientific, engineering, and organizational contexts.

A human-constructed framework in cognitive psychology for the process by which humans learn and develop new abilities through practice, instruction, and experience. Built to persist through pedagogical models, training programs, and the taxonomy of learning and development in educational psychology.

A human-made machine learning paradigm wherein a model performs tasks or classifies instances it has never encountered during training, without any task-specific examples. The concept relies on transfer of knowledge from related source domains and rich feature representations learned during pretraining. It emerged as a formal concept within representation learning and natural language processing, building on the broader paradigm of machine learning.

A human-made computational method for producing new data samples that follow the statistical patterns of training data. Built to persist through software implementations and mathematical formalism in probability theory and machine learning.

a human-made software system that retrieves information from a structured or unstructured corpus in response to user queries, using indexing, ranking algorithms, and query processing to surface relevant results

a human-made representational technique that maps discrete objects — words, items, or symbols — into continuous vector spaces where semantic or relational structure is preserved as geometric proximity
A human-made information retrieval technique that locates relevant documents by measuring semantic similarity between query and document representations, rather than matching literal keywords.

A human-invented mathematical and computational concept where data is encoded such that most elements are zero or negligible, used in signal processing, machine learning, and compressed sensing to enable efficient computation and capture structural priors

A human-designed construct that organizes and evaluates the totality of interaction between a person and a system — encompassing perception, emotion, and usability. Built to persist through design frameworks, evaluation methods, and the discipline of UX that makes subjective experience measurable and actionable.

A human-designed blueprint specifying the arrangement and connectivity of layers, neurons, and operations in a neural network. Built to persist through documentation, research papers, and implementation frameworks that describe how information flows through artificial neural systems.

A human-designed blueprint specifying the structure, components, connectivity, and organizational principles of a computational, statistical, or conceptual model. Built to persist through design specifications, documentation, and implementations.

A class of neural network architecture built around self-attention mechanisms, enabling parallel processing of sequential data and capturing long-range dependencies through weighted relationships between all positions in a sequence.

A human-made neural network mechanism that enables each position in a sequence to attend to every other position through computed weighted relationships — a designed information-routing primitive that persists through implementation frameworks and research literature.

A human-made statistical model that assigns probabilities to sequences of symbols (words or tokens), enabling prediction, generation, and interpretation of natural language — built to persist through parameterized weights, training data, and deployment infrastructure.

A human-made evaluation technique in machine learning where a trained model is tested on tasks or classes it was not explicitly trained for, built to persist through standardized benchmarks and model documentation

A bounded buffer of tokens that a language model can attend to in a single forward pass — a design parameter of transformer architectures that constrains the span of co-reference and long-range dependency the model can capture. Human-made as an engineered constraint on model capacity, persisted through architecture specifications and training protocols.

A human-made parameter in language model generation that scales logits before softmax sampling, controlling the randomness of token selection. Built to persist through implementation in inference frameworks (transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp), documentation of sampling behavior, and the statistical physics concept it borrows from (Gibbs/Boltzmann distributions).

A human-made model compression technique that reduces the numerical precision of a neural network's weights and activations (e.g., from FP32 to INT8 or lower), enabling faster inference and reduced memory usage on constrained hardware. Built to persist through standardized algorithms, open-source libraries, and deployment tooling.

The human-made cognitive category for storing general knowledge, facts, concepts, and meanings independent of personal experience. A framework built by cognitive psychology to classify memory types, persistent through academic teaching, research, and clinical practice.

A human-made neural network module that maps each input vector to an output through two linear transformations with a non-linear activation between them. Used as the per-position transformation component in transformer architectures, it extends representational capacity beyond linear attention by introducing pointwise non-linearity.

a human-designed method of injecting sequential position information into model representations, enabling architectures without inherent sequential bias to distinguish the relative or absolute position of elements in a sequence

The cognitive process of accessing and bringing stored information to conscious awareness. Human-made as a scientific concept: the map of the faculty of recall, distinct from the natural memory process itself. Central to learning science as both a demonstration and strengthening mechanism.

A mode of failure in generative AI systems where the model produces outputs that are factually incorrect, internally inconsistent, or entirely ungrounded in the provided context, yet presented with confidence. Human-made as a diagnostic concept in ML safety research — the map of a specific reliability failure mode, not the natural phenomenon of sensing something that isn't there.

The human-made architectural principle of reusing the same parameters (weights) across multiple parts of a model or system. Originating in convolutional neural networks where spatial locality means the same feature detector scans all regions, extended to transformer architectures and beyond. The concept is a deliberate design pattern for efficiency, generalization, and inductive bias.

The human-made technique of reducing numerical precision in computational models (e.g., mapping float32 parameters to int8) to decrease model size and inference cost while preserving behavioral approximation.
The key-value cache in transformer models — precomputed key and value vectors from earlier tokens, stored to avoid recomputation during autoregressive generation

A human-made ranking technique that reorders an initial set of results to improve relevance quality. It is built as a post-processing step in information retrieval and recommendation systems, applying a more sophisticated scoring function to a previously narrowed candidate set to produce a final ordered output.

A human-made liturgical form: a short hymn or poem of praise, especially one drawn from scripture. It is built by religious textual tradition and sustained through liturgical practice and canonical collections.

A human-made barrier structure designed to open and close within a wall, fence, or enclosure, controlling passage while the wall provides continuous boundary. Built of materials and sustained by maintenance, gates persist through physical construction and social convention about who may pass.

A human-made system of written symbols (graphemes) where each symbol represents a unit of sound (phoneme) in a spoken language. The alphabet distinguishes itself from syllabaries and logographies by decomposing speech into its smallest sound units and assigning one symbol per phoneme. This construct exists as a cultural technology — a map of spoken language encoded in marks — sustained by education, written records, and institutional teaching.
A caching mechanism is a human-designed system for storing copies of frequently or soon-needed data in a location optimized for rapid access, replacing direct retrieval from a slower primary store.

The human-designed practice of ensuring that AI system behavior, goals, and decision-making processes correspond to human intentions, values, and safety requirements. It is a field of engineering and research, not a natural property of systems.

Lossy compression is a human-made data encoding method that reduces file size by permanently eliminating redundant or less-important information, accepting some loss of fidelity in exchange for significantly smaller output. It is built to persist through standardized algorithms (JPEG, MP3, MPEG) that define what information is preserved and what is discarded.

A learning paradigm where neural networks acquire capabilities from examples provided in the input context at inference time, without updating model parameters. Human-made through transformer architecture design that uses self-attention to condition outputs on input sequences. Persists through architectural design choices and training methodology that make context-conditioned generalization possible.
A software-engineering practice that uses mathematical methods to prove or disproove that a system satisfies specified properties, replacing empirical testing with rigorous proof.

A human-made organizational practice that moves technology, knowledge, or innovations from their origin (e.g., research labs, universities) to new contexts where they are applied, commercialized, or scaled (e.g., industry, other sectors). Built to persist through institutional structures, licensing, and collaborative frameworks.

Function calling is the human-made pattern of instructing language models to produce structured output (typically JSON) that specifies which pre-defined function to invoke and with what arguments. It persists through API specifications, schema definitions (JSON Schema, OpenAPI), and the tool-use protocol that allows models to interact with external systems — a design pattern established by the model developers and adopted by application builders to extend model capabilities beyond text generation.

The human-made practice of having an AI system review, critique, and revise its own outputs before delivering them — a prompting technique that introduces a metacognitive step where the model evaluates its reasoning, identifies errors, and produces a corrected version.

The human-made mathematical framework for representing causal relationships among variables using systems of simultaneous equations. Developed in economics (Simpson, 1920s) and social sciences (Wright, 1934s), it enables estimation of direct, indirect, and total effects. Built to persist through computational tools, statistical software implementations, and formal notation in empirical research.

A human-made statistical concept for an unobserved variable inferred from observed measurements through mathematical modeling. Used to capture constructs that cannot be directly measured — such as intelligence, socioeconomic status, or psychological traits — enabling quantitative analysis of abstract phenomena.

A human-made statistical construct that specifies the mathematical relationship between latent (unobserved) variables and their observed indicators. Built to translate abstract theoretical constructs into measurable quantities for empirical research.

The scientific discipline studying cyclic and seasonal biological events in organisms — such as flowering, migration, and breeding — in relation to climate and environmental factors. A human-made field of observation and classification, not the biological events themselves.

The human-made process of translating informal concepts, practices, or knowledge into formal, explicit representations — using mathematical notation, logical symbols, or structured languages. Built to persist through documentation, teaching, and institutional practice, enabling precision and reproducibility.

The scientific study of how health-related conditions — disease, injury, disability, death — are distributed across populations and what factors determine those distributions. A human-made discipline built on systematic data collection, statistical reasoning, and field investigation to identify causes, prevent harm, and guide public health policy.

A human-made cognitive construct classifying memories that can be consciously recalled and declared — facts, events, and knowledge stored in the mind. Divided into semantic (general knowledge) and episodic (personal experiences) subtypes. The concept enables systematic organization of recallable information and distinguishes conscious from unconscious (procedural) memory systems. Built to persist through encoding, consolidation, and retrieval mechanisms.

A human-made epistemological framework positing that knowledge claims are justified by their grounding in observable, sensory experience. It constructs a method for evaluating beliefs through empirical evidence, standing in contrast to rationalist frameworks that privilege a priori reasoning. The MAP — the category of empiricist theories, their criteria, and their history — is human-made.

A human-made method of drawing conclusions under uncertainty, grounded in probability theory and formalized through mathematical frameworks. Built to persist via teaching, publication, and computational implementation.

A human-made concept describing the force multiplication achieved by machines to overcome loads, quantified as output-force-to-input-force ratio. Built to persist via engineering education, technical documentation, and computational design tools.

A human-made mechanical concept describing the pivot point about which a lever rotates to achieve mechanical advantage. Built to persist via engineering education, technical manuals, and practical mechanical design tradition.

A human-made activity engaged in for its own sake, characterized by voluntary participation, internal goals, and intrinsic enjoyment. Play is a structured form of free activity that extends human capacities for exploration, social bonding, and skill development, and is distinguished from work by the absence of external compulsion or utilitarian necessity.

A pulley is a simple machine consisting of a grooved wheel mounted on an axle, designed to redirect tension in a rope or cable and provide mechanical advantage when lifting or moving loads. It is a human-made artifact, constructed from materials such as wood, metal, or composite, and persists as both a physical tool and a conceptual component of classical mechanics.

A wedge is a human-made simple machine consisting of a triangular-shaped tool with a thick end that tapers to a thin edge, designed to split, lift, or tighten objects by concentrating force onto a small area. It is a human output: a manufactured artifact with specific geometry for mechanical work.

A human-made mechanical concept: a flat sloping surface that reduces required force by trading distance for magnitude. The concept — not the natural slope — is what qualifies. Persisted through physics education, engineering design, and tool geometry specification.

A human-made physical concept: the measure of rotational force — the tendency of a force to rotate an object about an axis or pivot. The concept (not the natural tendency of matter) qualifies. Persisted through mathematical formalism, engineering practice, and physics education.

A human-made laundry artifact: a corrugated or ribbed flat surface designed to increase friction when fabric is rubbed against it, amplifying hand-washing action. The concept (not any particular washboard) qualifies. Persists through manufacturing practice and material culture.

A human-made mechanical component: a rotating circular or cylindrical element with teeth cut around its perimeter, designed to mesh with another gear or rack to transmit torque, rotational motion, or linear motion. The concept (not any particular gear) qualifies. Persists through engineering practice, manufacturing, and mechanical design.

A human-made mechanical construct: a tapered cylinder or pin with a spiral ridge (thread) wound around its surface, designed to convert rotational motion into linear force or to fasten materials together by penetrating and gripping. The concept (not any particular screw) qualifies as the map. It persists through the concept's continued use in engineering practice and mechanical design.

A human-made mechanical element: a rotating or sliding piece with an irregular contour (the cam profile), designed to convert continuous rotational motion into a prescribed reciprocating or oscillating motion in a mating follower. The concept is built to persist through engineering design, manufacturing specifications, and technical teaching — the map of how shape controls motion.

A human-made mechanical construct: two concentric circular elements fixed together to rotate as one unit, designed to amplify rotational force — a small wheel attached to a larger axle so that force applied to one produces amplified torque on the other.

A human-made system: an assembly of mechanisms, components, and structures designed and built to perform specific tasks — amplifying force, transforming energy, or automating work. Built to persist through engineering design, materials science, and manufacturing.

A rack is a human-made mechanical component: a straight, toothed bar that meshes with a circular gear (pinion) to convert rotational motion into linear motion, or vice versa. Built to persist through standardized manufacturing (ISO tooth profiles, module systems) and engineering apprenticeship.

A human-made mechanical part designed to perform a specific function within a machine or mechanism: gears, cams, shafts, bearings, springs, linkages. Built to persist through repeated cycles of stress and motion within engineered systems. Manufactured from matter to extend human capacity for force transformation and motion control.

An actuator is a human-engineered component that converts stored energy (electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, or thermal) into controlled physical motion (linear, rotary, or oscillatory). It is a manufactured device — not a natural phenomenon — designed to execute commands from a control system by producing force and displacement within mechanical assemblies.

A human-made mechanical element consisting of an elastic material shaped to store mechanical energy through deformation and release it on demand — used in countless mechanisms from watches to vehicles to writing instruments.
a song sung to soothe a child to sleep — a human-made vocal form created for the specific purpose of calming and inducing sleep
rhythmic repetitive singing or speech, often in ritual, ceremonial, or devotional contexts — a human-made vocal form distinguished by its regularity and purpose

Attunement is a human-made practice and cultural skill — the deliberate effort to align one's emotional, cognitive, or behavioral state with another person or environment. It is not a natural faculty but a learned technique, transmitted through teaching, modeling, and social reinforcement.

A whistle is a human-made acoustic device — a simple tube or chamber that produces a clear tone when air is forced through it. It is an artifact, not a natural sound, designed and built to extend the range and character of human vocal communication.

A tangent is a mathematical construct — a line that touches a curve at exactly one point, sharing the same slope. It is a human-defined geometric concept, not a natural object, designed and formalized to characterize local behavior of curves.

A human-developed problem-solving technique that uses practical, experience-based rules of thumb, shortcuts, or educated guesses rather than guaranteed algorithms. Built to persist through teaching, documentation, and repeated application across domains from crafts to medicine to computing.

A human-made rhetorical concept for a deliberate departure from a main topic in speech or writing to pursue a related but non-essential idea. Built to persist through teaching, analysis of discourse, and the study of narrative structure.

A human-made garment accessory worn at the crotch area of the lower torso, designed and produced through tailoring and fashion practice. Built to persist through cultural tradition, fashion history, and the material culture of dress.

A human-made dispute resolution process in which a neutral third party facilitates structured negotiation between disputing parties to reach a voluntary, mutually acceptable agreement. Built to persist through legal institutions, organizational practice, and professional training traditions that sustain the role of the mediator and the method itself.

A human-made hollow resonator — typically a cast-metal cup or chamber — struck to produce a sustained tone. Built to persist through manufacturing practice and cultural tradition as an instrument of signaling, timekeeping, and ritual.

A human-made speech act in which a speaker commits to a future action or state of affairs, creating a normative expectation that the commitment will be fulfilled. Built to persist through social practice, memory, and the accountability structures that enforce or repair broken promises.

A human-made container consisting of a folded sheet of flexible material (paper, parchment, or synthetic) designed to enclose and protect written communication during transit. Built to persist through institutional adoption in postal systems and commercial packaging, it standardizes the transmission of correspondence across distance.

A human-made reference work — a systematically compiled directory of geographical place names paired with descriptive information (location, features, significance). Built to persist as a published reference enabling place-finding and structured geographic knowledge.

A soundboard is a human-made flat panel — typically made of resonant wood — engineered to collect and amplify sound vibrations from strings or other sound sources and project them into the air. Found in acoustic string instruments like guitars, violins, and pianos, it is a precision-crafted component whose quality fundamentally determines the instrument's tonal character.

An anvil is a heavy metal block — typically cast iron or steel — designed as a stable work surface for forging, shaping, and hammering metal in blacksmithing and metalworking. It is a human-made tool built to persist across centuries of craft practice.

A human-made holding device consisting of two jaws and a mechanism to draw them together under pressure, used to secure objects in place during work or storage. Built from rigid materials (metal, wood, plastic) with a tightening mechanism (screw, lever, spring, or toggle) to generate and maintain clamping force.

A human-made vocal technique producing sound through closed lips and steady airflow, used for self-soothing, musical accompaniment, or non-verbal communication. A deliberate act of sound production, distinct from natural sounds or speech.

A human-made oven constructed for firing ceramics, brick, or other materials at high temperature. Built from refractory materials, it is an artifact of the fired-materials tradition — the controlled application of heat to permanently transform materials through sintering, vitrification, or calcination. A human-made construct, not a geological feature.

The concept framework humans use to categorize and reason about the phenomenon of vibrational amplification when driven frequency matches a system's natural frequency. Built by physics, acoustics, and psychology as a map of a natural phenomenon — the concept itself, not the physical vibration, is human-made. The map persists through teaching, mathematical formalism, and cross-domain application (from instrument design to social cohesion).

A human-made concept for categorizing sounds produced by the human voice — the map of vocal sounds, not the sounds themselves. Includes hum, whistle, chant, speech, song, and other organized vocal output. Built to persist through language and teaching.
A human-made concept for a character virtue involving modest assessment of one's own importance, limitations, and fallibility — the map, not the natural disposition.

A human-made concept for the state of tension arising from incompatible or conflicting elements — applied in acoustics to describe clashing frequencies, in psychology to describe conflicting beliefs, and in any domain where mutually inconsistent components produce strain.

A human-made concept: a concise narrative constructed to teach a moral or spiritual lesson. Built to persist through oral and written teaching across generations, embedded in religious, educational, and literary traditions.
A human-made concept: a symbolic reminder of mortality, designed to prompt reflection on life's finitude. Built to persist through art, architecture, ritual, and cultural practice across generations.

A human-made concept: a class of mechanical devices or components designed to join or secure objects together. Built to persist as a technical category across engineering, construction, and everyday craft through standardized forms and principles.

A human-made concept: the mathematical and physical category of periodic variation around a central equilibrium value. Built to persist through physics, engineering, mathematics, and signal processing as a foundational model for understanding waves, vibration, and alternating phenomena.

A human-made concept: the category of reflected sound waves that return to a listener with sufficient delay to be perceived as distinct from the original. Built to persist through acoustics, architecture, music, and everyday auditory experience.

A human-made concept: the model of a propagating disturbance that transfers energy through a medium or space without transferring matter. Built to persist through mathematical formalism and physical measurement across mechanics, acoustics, and electromagnetism.

A human-made concept: the category of invariance under transformation — the property that a configuration, object, or system retains its appearance or structure when subjected to a specified transformation (reflection, rotation, translation, permutation, etc.). Built to persist through mathematical group theory, visual art, natural science classification, and everyday perceptual categorization.

A beat is the periodic amplitude variation produced when two waves of slightly different frequencies superpose. As a concept, it is a human-made measurement technique: musicians tune by listening for beats, physicists measure unknown frequencies by comparing them to known ones, and the beat frequency directly reveals the difference between two sources. The map — naming, quantifying, and exploiting this interference pattern — is the construct.

The state of strain produced by opposing forces, influences, or demands — a construct that applies equally to material stress, musical dissonance, psychological conflict, and social friction. Tension is the measurable or felt gap between what is and what would relieve it.

The intensity of force applied per unit of area, extent, or scope — a construct that quantifies the push exerted by one system against another. From physics (pascals) to social dynamics (social pressure) to psychology (stress pressure), pressure measures the concentration of force seeking to produce change.

A human-made conceptual category from music theory and aesthetics: the state of harmonious combination where simultaneous sounds or elements blend without clashing. Consonance is the qualitative judgment that two or more tones produce a stable, pleasant fusion — it exists as a perceptual construct evaluated by trained listeners, not as a physical property of the sounds themselves.

A concept from philosophy and semiotics: a representation or copy that no longer refers to an original reality, but instead generates its own self-referential hyperreality. The simulacrum is a human-made category for analyzing how reproductions can displace and replace the real in culture, media, and discourse.

A human-made acoustic concept: a frequency component of a complex sound that is higher than the fundamental frequency. The overtone is a construct of spectral analysis and musical acoustics — humans built the concept to categorize and reason about the frequency structure of musical tones.

A human-made acoustic and music-theoretical concept: the ordered sequence of frequencies that are integer multiples of a fundamental frequency. It is a construct of spectral analysis and musical acoustics — humans built the harmonic series to model the physical structure of complex tones and to organize musical tuning systems.

A human-made analytical construct: a representation of the distribution of a quantity (amplitude, energy, or power) across a range of values such as frequency, wavelength, or mass. Built for spectral analysis in acoustics, optics, and signal processing; persists through notation, mathematical formalism, and instrumentation.

A human-made concept describing a state in which competing forces, influences, or tendencies are balanced such that no net change occurs. The concept is modeled mathematically and verified empirically across physics, chemistry, economics, and psychology — it is the map of stability that humans constructed to predict and control systems.

Pitch is a human-made perceptual construct — the mapping of sound frequency to a subjective experience of highness or lowness. It is a category built by music theory, acoustic science, and instrument design to organize the continuum of vibration rates into meaningful positions on a tonal axis. The concept persists through notation systems, tuning standards, and cross-cultural pitch classification frameworks.

Polyphony is a human-made musical construct — the practice of combining two or more independent melodic voices performed simultaneously. It is a category created by music theory and compositional practice to organize and describe contrapuntal musical texture.

A human-made mathematical concept measuring the rate of repetition in periodic phenomena — cycles, vibrations, or oscillations per unit time. Built to quantify and compare rhythmic patterns across physics, music, and signal processing.

A human-made musical concept — a sequence of pitched notes organized temporally to form a coherent, recognizable pattern. Built to carry musical expression, be sung or played as a unit, and persist in memory as a distinct musical identity.

A human-made psychological construct — a state of complete absorption in an activity, coined by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi to describe the quality of experience where attention is so fully engaged that self-consciousness recedes and action and awareness merge. Built to persist through psychological research, performance theory, and applied practice in education, sports, and creative work.

A human-made practice and institutional framework of adjusting pitch relationships to achieve a desired harmonic standard — encompassing both the techniques (temperaments, intervals, pitch calibration) and the shared reference systems (concert pitch, tuning standards) that allow musicians and instruments to align. Built to persist through standardization, teaching, and the material culture of instrument manufacture.

A human-made musical concept — a named, categorized measure of the distance between two pitches, defined by specific parameters: step count, quality classification (major, minor, perfect, augmented, diminished), and the frequency ratio or semitone count that distinguishes it. Built to persist through music theory, notation systems, and instrument design.

A human-made analytical concept — the overall shape of sound energy distribution across frequencies, defined by amplitude at frequency bands or harmonic partials. Built to persist through acoustic measurement, synthesizer design, and vocal tract analysis.

A human-made analytical concept — the shape of a signal's variation over time, defined by the mapping of amplitude (or other quantities) onto a temporal axis. Built to persist through waveform notation, oscilloscope display, digital audio workstations, and mathematical description. It is the map of signal morphology, not the signal itself.

A human-made analytical concept — a discrete unit of musical meaning, a thought within a musical discourse that has characteristic boundaries and internal coherence. Built to persist through notation, performance practice, and musicological analysis.

A human-made analytical concept — the phenomenon whereby a vibrating system produces not just a fundamental frequency but also integer multiples of that frequency. Built to persist through mathematical analysis, acoustic measurement, and musical notation.

A human-made acoustical concept for describing the resonant frequency bands of the vocal tract that shape vowel quality — peaks in spectral energy produced by vocal tract filtering. Persisted through acoustic analysis, phonetic notation, and speech science pedagogy.

A human-made signal processing concept for detecting the beginning of a sound event — the transient attack point where amplitude rises above the background. Persisted through audio analysis algorithms, music information retrieval systems, and musical notation transcription.

A human-made perceptual construct for quantifying the intensity of sound as experienced by a listener — the subjective magnitude of acoustic stimulus. Persisted through psychophysical scaling laws (Stevens' power law) and engineering metrics (phon, sone, dB SPL) that map physical amplitude to perceived intensity.

A human-constructed concept for quantifying the magnitude of oscillation or displacement in wave, signal, and periodic systems — the measured extent of variation from equilibrium that characterizes the intensity or strength of a phenomenon.

The human-made concept of energy dissipation in oscillating systems — the mechanism by which an oscillator's amplitude decreases over time due to friction, resistance, or radiation. Built to predict and control the decay of waves in engineering, acoustics, and structural design.

The human-made concept of the initial attack phase of a sound — the brief, high-energy onset period before the steady state or sustain of a tone. Built to analyze and synthesize sounds by segmenting them into temporally distinct phases, enabling audio processing, music information retrieval, and sound design.

The Fast Fourier Transform is a human-made algorithm for computing the Discrete Fourier Transform efficiently — converting a time-domain signal into its frequency-domain representation. Built as a computational procedure for spectral analysis, it persists through standardized implementations in software libraries and hardware accelerators used in audio processing, signal analysis, and scientific computing.

The Discrete Fourier Transform is a human-made mathematical transformation that converts a finite sequence of time-domain samples into frequency-domain coefficients. Built to persist through computational practice, taught in signal processing curricula, and implemented as a standard algorithm in software libraries worldwide.

Phase is a human-made mathematical concept describing the position of a point within a cycle of a periodic waveform. Built to persist through signal processing, acoustics, and electrical engineering as a measure of relative timing between oscillations.

The attack is a human-made concept in acoustics and sound synthesis describing the initial phase of a sound — the time and manner in which a sound rises from silence to its peak amplitude. It is a parameter of the ADSR envelope model, designed to describe and control how sounds begin. Built to persist through teaching in music, audio engineering, and synthesis.

The impulse-response is a human-made concept in signal processing and systems theory that describes how a linear time-invariant system reacts to a brief input pulse (the Dirac delta function). It serves as a complete characterization of the system — knowing the impulse-response allows prediction of the system's output for any input via convolution. It is a map, not a physical thing: the impulse itself is an idealization, and the response is a model built by engineers to analyze, design, and predict system behavior.

A human-made concept in audio and signal processing that models how the amplitude of a sound or signal changes over time. Built to persist through formal notation (ADSR), mathematical modeling, and measurement instruments in music theory and engineering.

A human-made concept in physics and engineering that models the irreversible transformation of organized energy into disordered thermal energy. Built to persist through thermodynamic formalism, entropy accounting, and engineering loss budgets.

A human-made concept in mathematics and signal processing that models the combination of two functions to produce a third — specifically, how a signal's shape is transformed by a system's impulse response, and more broadly how one function's structure warps or filters another. Built to persist through integral and summation formulas, enabling analysis of linear systems, probability distributions, and spatial transformations.

A human-made concept in electrical engineering and signal processing that represents a sinusoidal signal as a rotating complex number, encoding both amplitude and phase into a single mathematical entity. Built to persist through complex arithmetic, enabling compact analysis of AC circuits, oscillators, frequency-domain signal transformations, and modulation schemes.

Overshoot is a human-made concept in signal processing and control theory that quantifies the extent to which a system's response exceeds its intended steady-state value following a step input or disturbance. It is built as a named metric to characterize and compare the dynamic behavior of engineered systems — from electronic filters to mechanical suspensions — and persists through mathematical formalism, engineering standards, and design practice.

A filter is a human-made signal-processing construct that selectively passes or attenuates frequency components of a signal. It is designed and implemented — whether as an electronic circuit, digital algorithm, or mechanical device — to shape the spectral content of signals for specific applications.

A human-made concept in signal processing that quantifies the displacement of a periodic waveform relative to a reference, expressed in degrees or radians. It is built to persist through mathematical formalism and engineering practice across communications, audio, and control systems.

A human-made concept in signal processing and systems theory that specifies the range of frequencies a system passes, attenuates, or analyzes. It is built to persist as a design parameter and analytical measure — used to characterize filters, channels, instruments, and physical systems by the span of frequencies over which they operate effectively.

Group-delay is the negative derivative of phase response with respect to angular frequency, measuring how long different frequency components of a signal are delayed as they pass through a system. It quantifies the time lag of the signal's energy envelope. Human-made through signal processing and communications theory; persists through filter design, audio engineering, and network analysis.

Step-response is the output of a system when subjected to a step input — a sudden change from one constant level to another. It is a human-made analytical construct used to characterize system dynamics, transient behavior, and settling properties. Built to persist through mathematical formalization and engineering practice.

A frequency-response is a human-made analytical construct used in signal processing and control engineering to describe how a system's output varies as a function of input frequency. It is maintained through engineering practice, measurement instrumentation (network analyzers, spectrum analyzers), and theoretical frameworks — enabling designers to predict and shape system behavior across frequency bands.

A human-made analytical concept in electrical engineering that extends the notion of resistance to alternating-current (AC) circuits by representing opposition to current as a complex quantity — real part resistance, imaginary part reactance — which varies with frequency. Built to characterize and predict how circuit elements and networks respond to time-varying signals.

A human-made technique in signal processing that applies a mathematical function (window) to a finite segment of a signal before transforming it, reducing spectral leakage caused by abrupt signal truncation. It is maintained through algorithmic implementation and engineering practice, with window shapes (Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Kaiser) chosen based on the trade-off between main-lobe width and side-lobe suppression.

A human-made analytical concept in electrical engineering that represents the imaginary component of impedance, quantifying frequency-dependent opposition to alternating current arising from energy storage elements (inductors and capacitors) rather than energy dissipation.

A human-made analytical concept in signal processing that describes the spreading of spectral energy into adjacent frequency bins when a finite-duration signal segment is analyzed with a Fourier transform, caused by the implicit rectangular truncation of the signal.

Ringing is the human concept of sustained oscillations that persist after a transient disturbance in a dynamic system. It arises when a system has overshoot and insufficient damping, causing the output to oscillate around the steady-state value before settling. Engineers and physicists model ringing as the underdamped response of second-order systems, and it is a practical concern in electronics, control theory, and acoustics where unwanted oscillations can degrade performance or cause damage.

The sinc function is a human-defined mathematical construct — the normalized form sin(πx)/(πx) — used throughout Fourier analysis, signal processing, and numerical interpolation. It arises as the Fourier transform of a rectangular window and as the impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter.

The artifact produced when a signal is sampled at insufficient rate, causing higher-frequency components to masquerade as lower ones. Human-made concept from sampling theory; it arises from the mathematics of discrete-time representation and is engineered against in ADC design, anti-aliasing filter specification, and digital audio/video pipelines.

A human-made mathematical construct — a function designed to taper a signal's amplitude at the edges of a finite segment, reducing spectral artifacts in frequency-domain analysis. Built to persist through use in signal processing, communications, and audio engineering.

A mathematical rule in signal processing: to perfectly reconstruct a continuous signal from samples, the sampling rate must exceed twice the signal's highest frequency component. Human-made theorem from sampling theory; built to persist as a formal constraint in information and signal theory.

A human-made signal-processing technique: appending zeros to the end of a discrete signal before computing its Fourier transform, to improve interpolated frequency resolution in the spectral estimate. Built to persist through digital signal processing practice and standards.
A human-made signal-processing circuit or algorithm designed to attenuate frequency components above half the sampling rate, preventing aliasing artifacts during discretization
A human-made mathematical representation that distributes the power of a signal across its frequency components, revealing the spectral energy density of a signal or time series.

A human-made mathematical concept that quantifies the ability of a spectral analysis method (such as the DFT) to distinguish between two closely spaced frequency components. It is determined by the observation time, window function, and sampling parameters — a construct of human signal processing theory.

A human-made mathematical representation that quantifies the distribution of signal power (or energy) across frequency, expressed as power per unit bandwidth. It is a construct of spectral analysis theory, used to characterize the frequency content of deterministic and stochastic signals.

A human-made mathematical transformation that decomposes a function or signal into its constituent frequency components. It is built to persist as a formal tool in mathematical analysis and signal processing, encoded through the Fourier integral and discrete Fourier transform.

A human-made model for the time-domain behavior of systems following a sudden change in input — the overshoot, ringing, and settling that occurs before the system reaches steady state. Built to persist through engineering practice, simulation, and education.

A human-made window function defined by the formula w(n) = 0.54 - 0.46*cos(2*pi*n/(N-1)), designed to reduce spectral leakage in spectral analysis by tapering signal edges. It persists as a standardized mathematical construct in signal processing textbooks and software libraries.

A human-made method of examining the frequency composition of signals by decomposing them into their constituent frequency components. It persists as a practice built on mathematical frameworks (Fourier transforms, window functions) and is sustained through engineering discipline, computational tools, and scientific literature.

The human-made concept describing the gradual decay of oscillations in a system after excitation ceases, characterized by amplitude decay rate and frequency content, used in acoustics, electrical engineering, and mechanical systems analysis.

The human-made concept of a system property where the output scales proportionally with input (homogeneity) and responses to multiple inputs add together (superposition), forming the foundation of linear system analysis in engineering and physics.

The human-made concept describing the frequency-dependent time shift that a system imposes on signal components — the angular part of the frequency response, measured in radians or degrees, used to characterize dispersion and distortion in filters and communication channels.

The human-made concept describing the integral transform that maps a time-domain function to a complex frequency-domain representation, enabling analysis of linear systems through algebraic manipulation of differential equations

The human-made practice and methodology of designing filters — devices or algorithms that selectively pass or reject frequency components of signals. It combines mathematical analysis, simulation, and practical implementation to achieve specified frequency response characteristics.

The human-made specification and methodology for determining the minimum frequency separation at which two distinct signal components can be distinguished in a spectrum. It is a parameter of measurement systems, defined by the analysis method (e.g., Fourier transform window length), and persists through engineering standards, instrument specifications, and the mathematical theory of signal analysis.

The human-made measure of the center of mass of a frequency spectrum — a weighted average of spectral components where frequencies are weighted by their magnitude. It is a quantitative descriptor used in audio analysis, signal processing, and acoustic feature extraction to characterize the timbral brightness of a signal.

The human-made signal processing construct that transforms a spectrum back into a spectral-like domain (quefrency) by taking the logarithm of the power spectrum and applying an inverse Fourier transform. It separates source and filter components in signals — used in speech analysis for pitch detection, vibration diagnosis for fault detection, and deconvolution — revealing periodic structures in spectra that are invisible in the frequency domain.
