The human-made signal processing technique that reverses the effects of convolution — given an observed signal that is a convolution of an unknown source with a known kernel, deconvolution applies mathematical procedures to recover an estimate of the original source.
A time-varying visual display of a signal's frequency content over time, produced by human signal-processing methods to make spectral evolution observable

A signal-processing method that divides a time-varying signal into short overlapping segments and applies the Fourier transform to each, producing a localized frequency representation that varies with time.

The independent variable of a cepstrum analysis, representing time-like delay in the quefrency domain; the term is a back-formation from 'frequency' to indicate that cepstral analysis operates on a transformed time axis derived from the logarithm of the power spectrum.

A human-made signal-processing construct that encodes a signal's energy distribution across both time and frequency dimensions simultaneously, enabling analysis of non-stationary signals whose frequency content varies over time

A human-made signal-processing construct representing the individual values in a cepstrum sequence — discrete coefficients that encode spectral envelope information, extracted by applying the Fourier transform to the logarithm of a power spectrum estimate. Widely used in speech recognition (MFCCs) and mechanical vibration analysis to isolate periodic structures in spectra.

Phase spectrum is a human-made signal-processing concept that represents the phase angles (timing relationships) of frequency components in a signal's frequency-domain representation. Paired with the magnitude spectrum, it fully characterizes the complex spectrum of a signal. It is the map of relative phase relationships constructed by Fourier analysis, not the natural phases of oscillation.

The magnitude spectrum of a signal is the function that assigns, to each frequency component in a spectral decomposition, the amplitude (modulus) of the corresponding complex-valued spectral coefficient. It is obtained by applying a frequency-domain transform and extracting the absolute value of the resulting complex output — complementing the phase spectrum, which records phase angles. The magnitude spectrum encodes the energy distribution of a signal across frequencies; it determines the relative strength of each frequency component but alone cannot reconstruct the signal's waveform without the accompanying phase spectrum. It persists as a theoretical construct in signal analysis, spectroscopy, and spectral estimation.

The technique of transforming a signal's spectral representation into a quefrency-domain representation to reveal periodic structure within the spectrum. It operates by computing the inverse Fourier transform of the logarithm of the magnitude spectrum, producing a questral-domain signal where quefrency measures the periodicity of spectral components. Human-made through mathematical formalism, persisted in signal processing literature and applied in speech recognition, seismic deconvolution, and mechanical vibration analysis.

The human-made system of mathematical operations — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and their generalizations — built to compute, quantify, and transform numerical quantities. Designed and formalized across civilizations as a tool for calculation, measurement, and abstract reasoning.

The human-made discipline of analyzing, modifying, and synthesizing signals — mathematical representations of information — to extract meaning, compress data, or produce desired outputs. Built through algorithms, hardware, and mathematical theory to operate on audio, images, communications, sensor data, and more.

The human-made mathematical transform that converts a finite sequence of equally-spaced samples of a function into a same-length sequence of equally-spaced values representing frequency components. Built through the discrete sampling theorem and computational algorithms, designed to bridge continuous and digital signal processing.

The human-made quantitative measure that compares the level of a desired signal to the level of background noise. Built as a dimensionless ratio to characterize signal quality in communications, audio, imaging, and measurement systems. Persists through engineering standards, mathematical definitions, and instrument calibration.

A human-made mathematical construct: the individual values obtained as output of the cepstrum computation — the amplitude of the inverse Fourier transform of the log-power spectrum, each indexed by quefrency. Built to persist through notation in signal processing, audio analysis, and diagnostic engineering, where cepstral coefficients serve as feature representations for classification and pattern detection.
A human-made methodology that applies statistical methods — probability theory, inference, estimation — to examine data, test hypotheses, and draw conclusions about patterns and variability.

Human-made feature extraction technique that computes Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients from audio signals. Built by designing a triangular Mel-scale filterbank over the power spectrum, taking log energy, then applying DCT — a standardized pipeline for speech and audio analysis.

Human-made mathematical representation space in which cepstral coefficients live. Created by taking the log of the power spectrum and transforming via inverse Fourier transform — a construct used exclusively in signal processing and speech analysis.

Human-made perceptual scale that maps audio frequencies (Hz) to a linear scale (mels) based on human pitch perception. Created by Stevens, Volkmann, and Newman (1937) through psychoacoustic experiments. Built to persist as a standardized mapping function used in audio processing standards, speech recognition pipelines, and music information retrieval software.
Human-made array of triangular filterbanks spaced according to the mel frequency scale, used for spectral energy extraction in speech recognition and audio processing.

Human-made concept in acoustics and music theory for integer multiples of a fundamental frequency. A harmonic is a tone whose frequency equals n×f₀ where n is a positive integer and f₀ is the fundamental. Used in instrument design, tuning systems, spectral analysis, and voice classification — persists through notation, teaching, and mathematical formalism across musical and physical disciplines.

Human-made system and methodology for automatically converting spoken language into text or other structured representations. Built from signal processing, linguistics, and machine learning to persist as a practical technology and research field.

A signal processing technique that modifies cepstral coefficients to shape the spectral envelope of a signal. It is human-made: a mathematical procedure implemented in DSP algorithms for speech synthesis, voice conversion, and spectral smoothing. The technique persists through standardized algorithms in speech processing toolkits and research literature.

A signal processing feature that counts how often a discrete-time signal crosses zero amplitude within a fixed window. It is human-made: a numerical metric computed by DSP algorithms for audio analysis, music information retrieval, and speech processing. The technique persists through standardized implementations in audio analysis libraries (librosa, LibROSA, MATLAB) and research protocols. Zero-crossing rate is used to distinguish voiced from unvoiced speech, detect transients, and classify musical instruments.

A signal processing feature that measures the rate of change of the power spectrum over time. It is human-made: a numerical metric computed by DSP algorithms for audio analysis, music information retrieval, and speech processing. The technique persists through implementations in audio analysis libraries (librosa, Essentia) and research protocols. Spectral flux is used for onset detection, rhythm analysis, audio segmentation, and distinguishing voiced from unvoiced speech segments.

A signal processing feature that measures how sinusoidal (tonal) versus noise-like a power spectrum is. It is human-made: a mathematical metric computed by DSP algorithms for audio analysis, speech processing, and music information retrieval, implemented as the geometric mean divided by the arithmetic mean of spectral power values.

A human-made signal processing technique for separating convolutional and multiplicative components in signals. Introduced by Oppenheim and Sheiner 1967, it transforms signals into a domain where convolution becomes addition via logarithm, applies a linear filter, then transforms back. Persisted through textbook treatment in digital signal processing, implementation in deconvolution, image enhancement, speech processing, and radar signal separation.

A human-made speech enhancement technique that estimates noise in the cepstral domain and subtracts it from the speech cepstrum to reduce noise. Introduced by Boll (1979). It separates additive noise from speech by operating in quefrency space where noise and speech components become additively separable, enabling targeted noise reduction.

A human-made signal processing feature that quantifies the tonal contrast of a spectrum by measuring the energy difference between spectral peaks and valleys within defined frequency bands, computed via band-wise peak-to-valley analysis of a power spectrum.

A human-made audio signal processing feature that measures the frequency below which a specified percentage of total spectral energy is contained. Built for timbre characterization, music information retrieval, and audio analysis pipelines.

A human-made mathematical descriptor that quantifies the spread or width of a signal's frequency spectrum around its spectral centroid. It is computed from the power spectrum as the weighted standard deviation of frequency bins, where weights are the spectral magnitudes. Built for audio analysis, music information retrieval, and timbre characterization — it answers the question of how concentrated versus dispersed energy is across the frequency axis.

A human-made spectral representation that maps a signal's power spectrum onto the mel frequency scale using a triangular filterbank. It is computed by humans for audio analysis, speech recognition, and music information retrieval — designed to approximate human auditory perception of frequency.

A human-made signal representation encoding a signal's energy or amplitude distribution across frequency components. Computed by applying spectral analysis techniques (most commonly the Fourier transform and its variants) to transform time-domain signals into frequency-domain representations. Used in signal processing, audio analysis, and communications for characterizing the frequency content of signals.

Spectral-energy is a human-made analytical construct: the total power or energy integrated across a signal's frequency spectrum at a given time frame. It is computed by summing or integrating the spectral power distribution, serving as a fundamental feature in audio analysis, speech processing, and music information retrieval. As a mathematical abstraction, it exists only through human-defined computation and persists in analytical frameworks, software tools, and scientific practice.

Power spectral density (PSD) is a human-made analytical construct that describes how the power of a signal or time series is distributed across frequency components. It is computed as the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function (Wiener–Khinchin theorem) or by periodogram methods from finite data. PSD provides a map for understanding signal composition in the frequency domain, enabling engineers and scientists to identify dominant frequencies, bandwidth, and noise characteristics. Persisted through computation, visualization as spectral plots, and formal mathematical definition.

Periodogram is a human-made spectral estimation technique that computes the squared magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a signal as a non-parametric estimate of its power spectral density. It was introduced by Arthur Schuster in 1898 as a mathematical construct for analyzing periodicities in time series data, and persists through widespread use in signal processing, acoustics, and spectral analysis software.

A signal processing technique for estimating the frequency content of a signal from a finite set of samples. It encompasses methods — periodogram, Welch's method, Bartlett's method, parametric models — that convert time-domain data into frequency-domain representations of power distribution. The institution persists through standardized algorithms embedded in DSP libraries, instrumentation, and textbooks, forming the methodological backbone of audio analysis, communications, vibration monitoring, and spectral analysis.

A spectral estimation technique that reduces variance of the periodogram by dividing a signal into overlapping segments, computing a periodogram for each segment (with windowing), and averaging them. It trades frequency resolution for lower estimator variance, making it practical for real-world signals with noise.

A human-made spectral estimation technique that reduces periodogram variance by dividing a signal into non-overlapping segments, computing a periodogram for each segment, and averaging the results. Designed by M.S. Bartlett (1948) as a computationally simpler alternative to Welch's method.

A human-made theoretical construct in signal processing that defines the maximum frequency可 represented without aliasing when a continuous signal is sampled, equal to half the sampling rate. Built to persist through mathematical definition in information theory.

A human-made signal processing construct consisting of a set of parallel band-pass filters, each tuned to a specific frequency band, used to decompose a signal into its constituent spectral components. Built to persist through algorithmic implementation in digital signal processing and computational models.

A human-made signal processing construct that selects a specific frequency range from a broader signal, attenuating frequencies outside a defined lower and upper cutoff. Built as a filter circuit or algorithmic module to persist in communication systems, audio processing, and spectral analysis.

A human-made measurement instrument that displays the frequency-domain representation (amplitude or power vs. frequency) of a signal in real time or post-capture. Built as dedicated hardware or software, it translates time-domain signals into visible spectral plots using FFT or filter-bank decomposition.

A human-made spectral construct that represents the smooth envelope of a signal's spectrum, extracted through cepstral analysis by retaining only the low-quefrency cepstral coefficients. It captures gross spectral shape (spectral tilt, formant structure) while suppressing fine spectral detail and pitch harmonics. Built to persist as a computational feature in speech processing, audio analysis, and speaker identification systems.

A human-made signal processing construct: a local maximum in the amplitude spectrum of a signal, identified as a point where spectral energy rises above immediate neighbours. It encodes the perceptually salient frequencies — formants in speech, harmonics in music, resonant modes in mechanical systems — and is extracted by algorithms that detect sign-changes in the discrete derivative of the spectrum.

A human-made audio signal processing construct: a time-frequency representation obtained by first computing a short-time Fourier transform spectrogram and then warping the frequency axis onto the mel scale, a perceptual scale approximating human auditory frequency discrimination. It persists through standard DSP pipeline implementation and is the foundational intermediate representation for MFCC computation.

A human-made mathematical construct in signal processing and statistics: a measure of similarity between two signals as a function of time-lag applied to one of them. Built to persist as an algorithmic operation over discrete or continuous signals, enabling pattern matching, delay estimation, and template matching.

A human-made perceptual frequency scale that maps physical sound frequency (Hz) onto a scale linear below 1000 Hz and logarithmic above, approximating human pitch perception. It is a mathematical transformation prescribed by psychoacoustic research and embedded in audio processing algorithms, speech recognition pipelines, and music information retrieval systems — a standardized conceptual tool built to persist across disciplines.

A mathematical technique that maps physical frequencies from one frequency scale to another (e.g. linear Hz to perceptual mel scale). Implemented as a monotonic transform function in audio processing pipelines and psychoacoustic models. Persists through algorithmic specifications and software implementations in signal processing.

A human-made mathematical technique that converts a finite sequence of data samples into a sum of cosine functions with different frequencies and amplitudes. Specifically, it maps a signal of length N into N frequency components using only cosine basis functions, producing real-valued coefficients. Used extensively in signal compression (JPEG, MP3), feature extraction (MFCCs), and spectral analysis.

A human-made mathematical technique that decomposes a signal or function into its constituent frequency components. It carves the spectral representation as a mapping from time-domain (or spatial-domain) signal to frequency-domain coefficients, persisting through mathematical notation, algorithms (FFT, DFT), and computational implementations in signal processing software.

Short-Time Fourier Transform is a human-made mathematical technique for analyzing how the spectral content of a signal changes over time. It divides a signal into shorter overlapping segments, applies the Fourier transform to each, and assembles the results into a time-frequency representation.

Cepstral lifter (also called cepstral filter or lifter) is a human-made signal processing technique that operates in the cepstral (quefrency) domain. It applies filtering — low-pass, high-pass, or band-pass — to cepstral coefficients to separate different components of a signal: low-pass lifting extracts the slowly-varying spectral envelope (e.g., vocal-tract response), while high-pass lifting extracts the rapidly-varying residual (e.g., excitation source).

Spectral-feature is a human-made mathematical concept in signal processing and audio analysis. It refers to a numerical descriptor or characteristic extracted from a signal's spectral representation (power spectrum, cepstrum, or spectrogram) that quantifies a specific measurable aspect of the signal's frequency-domain structure. Examples include MFCCs, spectral centroid, spectral bandwidth, spectral rolloff, and spectral flatness. Built to persist as a category in the taxonomy of signal processing descriptors.

Furniture is a human-made category of movable objects intended to support various human activities such as seating, sleeping, storage, and work. It encompasses chairs, tables, beds, cabinets, and shelves, crafted through carpentry, upholstery, and industrial manufacturing processes. Furniture persists through material construction — joinery, fastening, finishing — and cultural design traditions.

Pitch-detection is a human-made computational technique that estimates the fundamental frequency (pitch) of an audio or speech signal. It persists through decades of DSP research, is implemented in music software and speech analysis tools, and is taught as a core concept in signal processing curricula.

Cepstral-coefficients is a human-made computational representation consisting of a sequence of numerical values in the quefrency domain that encode the spectral envelope and fine structure of a signal. It persists through decades of digital signal processing research and is implemented as the standard feature vector in speech recognition systems, audio classification pipelines, and machine learning models for acoustic analysis.

Liftering is a human-made signal processing technique in which a window function is applied to the cepstrum (the quefrency-domain representation of a signal) to selectively amplify or attenuate specific quefrency ranges. It is the quefrency-domain analogue of spectral filtering and is used for tasks like pitch extraction, noise reduction, and voice modification. The technique persists through mathematical formalism and implementation in DSP libraries.

The cepstral-transform is a human-made signal processing procedure that converts a time-domain signal into the quefrency domain representation. It consists of computing the FFT of a signal, taking the log of the magnitude spectrum, and applying the inverse FFT to produce the cepstrum. The procedure is algorithmically well-defined, taught in signal processing curricula, and implemented in software libraries worldwide — it persists as a standardized method of domain conversion.

A human-made signal processing technique for noise reduction that estimates the power spectrum of additive noise and subtracts it from the noisy signal spectrum, enabling cleaner signal reconstruction.

A human-made signal processing objective: the set of techniques designed to remove or attenuate unwanted noise from a signal while preserving the desired signal content. Noise reduction techniques include spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, cepstral subtraction, and adaptive filtering — each implementing a specific strategy for noise estimation and removal.

A perceptual frequency scale in hertz, designed to model human auditory perception, where equal-distance steps are perceived as equal pitch intervals. Human-made as a mathematical mapping (linear-to-mel transformation) and used persistently in speech processing and audio analysis for mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, spectrograms, and loudness modeling.

The quantitative measure of data transfer or representation rate — bits processed, transmitted, or stored per unit of time. Human-made as a standardized specification in telecommunications, digital audio, video encoding, networking, and data storage protocols.

The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words. Human-made as a theoretical construct in phonology, persisted through linguistic analysis, language teaching, speech technology, and the IPA (International Phonetic Association) classification system.

A time-frequency representation of a signal where the frequency axis is mapped to the mel scale to model human auditory perception. Human-made as a computational construct in signal processing and machine learning, persisted through software libraries (librosa, TensorFlow, PyTorch) and standardized as the dominant acoustic feature representation in speech recognition and audio classification pipelines.

A human-made signal processing technique for modeling digital signals as the output of a linear filter driven by an excitation source. Developed by Salomon Kullback, Robert Leibson, and J.L. Flanagan in 1951 for speech coding, and independently by B. S. Atal and Hanif R. Sandler in 1976 for speech analysis. Persisted through standardization in ITU-T G.729, 3GPP AMR, and decades of DSP implementations.

A human-made measure of dissimilarity between two spectral shapes, computed from the cepstral coefficients of each spectrum. The distance metric quantifies how different two spectra are in terms of their spectral envelope structure, enabling comparison of timbre, speaker identity, or material properties. Persisted as a mathematical formula implemented in software and DSP toolkits.

A human-made mathematical technique for decomposing signals into time-frequency components using scaled and shifted wavelet functions. Developed as a generalization of Fourier analysis, it provides multi-resolution analysis that captures both frequency and temporal information simultaneously, making it suitable for non-stationary signals.

A human-made music-theory concept that groups all pitches sharing the same pitch name (or related by octave equivalence) into a single equivalence class. Developed within 20th-century atonal theory and set theory, it abstracts away octave and timbre to focus on pitch relationships, forming the basis for pitch-class sets and tone rows.

A human-made frequency scale used in audio and music processing that maps linear frequencies to a perceptual scale approximating human hearing. Developed by Stevens, Volkmann, and Newman (1937), it is the foundation for mel-scale filtering and the mel-frequency cepstrum. Built to persist because it standardizes perceptually-motivated frequency representations across speech recognition, audio analysis, and music information retrieval.

A human-made method of representing or mapping frequencies along a non-linear or perceptual axis. Frequency scales abstract the physical property of frequency (Hertz) into forms useful for audio analysis, music theory, and hearing science. Built to persist because they standardize how instruments, software, and researchers represent pitch relationships and spectral distributions.

A human-made signal processing framework for analyzing how the frequency content of a signal changes over time. It produces a time-frequency representation (like a spectrogram or scalogram) that reveals non-stationary signal structure which pure spectral analysis cannot capture.

A human-made mathematical approach that represents data or signals using a fixed set of parameters optimized to fit observed measurements, built to persist through formal algorithms, published methods, and teaching in statistics, signal processing, and machine learning disciplines.

A human-made musical representation that maps audio energy to the 12 pitch classes of Western music, built to persist through feature-extraction algorithms used in music information retrieval, chord recognition, and timbral analysis.

A human-made signal processing technique that rebuilds a signal's frequency spectrum from a compact or modified representation, built to persist through iterative algorithms like Griffin-Lim that recover phase information lost during spectral compression.
